sections.title: Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment

blocks.text:
### Continuous Deployment

A team of five developers works on `orders-service` for six weeks, each on a separate branch. On the last day the branches are merged. Two branches changed the same entity class, a third upgraded a library that the other two use, and the combined code does not compile. Two further days pass before the build is green, and nobody can state which change introduced which defect. This situation is known as integration hell, and it is the problem that continuous integration was invented to remove.

A second problem appears after the merge. The release is built on a developer laptop, copied to a server by hand, and started with a script that exists only in one person's shell history. The release takes an afternoon, it fails in ways that differ from the previous release, and for that reason releases are postponed and grow larger. Larger releases are riskier, which postpones them further.

Continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment are three related practices that address these problems by making integration and release small, frequent, automated and repeatable. The reader is assumed to know Git (see the Part on Git and GitHub), to be able to build a Spring Boot application with Maven, and to know what a Docker image is (see the Part on containers). This chapter defines the terms precisely, describes the anatomy of a pipeline and introduces the measurements used to judge whether the practices work.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The integration problem

Integration cost grows with the time that changes stay unmerged and with the number of changes merged at once. A conflict between two changes of one day is resolved by the two authors in minutes, because both remember the intent. A conflict between two changes of six weeks requires reconstructing that intent from the code. Continuous integration reduces the interval between divergence and merge to hours.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: Continuous integration (CI): the practice of merging every developer's work into a shared mainline frequently (at least daily) and verifying each merge with an automated build and automated tests. A merge that breaks the build is treated as the most urgent problem of the team.

The practice has a human part and a tool part. The tool part is a CI server (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI) that starts a build for every push. The human part is the agreement that the mainline stays releasable: a failing build on the mainline is fixed or reverted immediately, and developers do not push further changes onto a red mainline. A CI server without that agreement only reports failures that nobody acts on.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: Continuous delivery: the practice of keeping the software in a state that can be released to production at any time, by passing every change through an automated pipeline that ends in a deployable artifact, which is deployed to production by a manual, one-click decision.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: Continuous deployment: continuous delivery in which the final manual decision is removed: every change that passes all automated stages is deployed to production without human approval.

The three terms form a ladder, shown in the next figure. Continuous integration is the base: build and test on every change. Continuous delivery extends the automation up to a release candidate that has been deployed to a production-like environment and is ready to ship. Continuous deployment automates the last step. The abbreviation CD is used for both delivery and deployment, so a sentence that uses it must state which is meant.

blocks.text:
Continuous deployment is not a goal in itself. A bank that must record a human approval for every production change practises continuous delivery by policy, and nothing is lost: the pipeline still produces a release candidate that can be approved within minutes. The common mistake is the opposite one, calling a build server that runs `mvn package` "CI/CD" while releases are still manual.

#### Anatomy of a pipeline

A pipeline is the automated sequence of stages that a change passes on its way to production. Each stage answers one question and either passes or stops the pipeline. The stages for `orders-service` are listed below. The grouping into commit, acceptance and release stages follows the terminology of the book Continuous Delivery by Jez Humble and David Farley (2010); the target durations are assumed values that the reader should replace with measurements from the own project.

Does each class behave as specified, in isolation?

blocks.caption: Pipeline stages for orders-service, with the question each stage answers.

blocks.text:
The order of stages is a cost-ordering: cheap and likely-to-fail checks run first. A compile error is detected in seconds, before 10 minutes are spent on integration tests. This principle is called failing fast, and it applies inside a stage as well: Maven stops at the first failed module unless told otherwise.

#### Principles that make the practice work

#### Fast feedback

A developer who waits 40 minutes for a verdict starts another task, and a failure then costs a context switch. A commonly cited target for the commit stage is about ten minutes (this figure is a guideline from the continuous delivery literature, not a rule). When the commit stage exceeds the target, the usual remedies are parallel jobs, dependency caching, splitting slow tests into a later stage and removing redundant work. Later chapters demonstrate each remedy.

#### Pipeline as code

The definition of the pipeline (stages, commands, environments) is stored in the repository next to the source, as a YAML file for GitHub Actions or a `Jenkinsfile` for Jenkins. Compared with a pipeline configured in a web interface, a pipeline as code has history (`git log` shows who changed the test command and why), is reviewed in pull requests, is reproduced by checking out an old commit, and is restored from the repository after a loss of the CI server.

#### Build once, deploy many

The artifact is built exactly once, at the start of the acceptance stage, and the same bytes are promoted through every environment. Only configuration differs between environments: database URL, credentials and feature settings are supplied at deployment time, not compiled in. If each environment were rebuilt from source, the tested binary and the deployed binary would be different artifacts that merely share a source commit, and a difference in a dependency, a JDK patch version or a build timestamp could invalidate the testing.

blocks.text:
#### Immutable artifacts and unique versions

An artifact that has been published is never modified. A new build produces a new version. For container images the identifier is the digest, `sha256:` followed by a hash of the image manifest, and a human-readable tag such as the Git commit SHA is attached to it. Re-pushing an existing tag with different content (for example `latest`) breaks traceability, because the name no longer identifies what ran in production. The chapter on registries in the Part on containers describes tagging strategies.

#### Environments

An environment is a place where the application runs with its own configuration, data and access rules. The three common ones are listed below.

blocks.text:
Staging earns its value only when it resembles production: the same JDK, the same container image, the same PostgreSQL major version and the same deployment script. A staging environment with an in-memory database finds defects that production does not have and misses those that it does.

#### Trunk-based development as the branching model of CI

Continuous integration requires branches that live for hours or at most a day or two. In trunk-based development all developers integrate into one main branch ("trunk"), either by committing directly or by short-lived branches merged through pull requests. Unfinished functionality is hidden behind a feature flag (a configuration switch that disables a code path at run time) so that incomplete work can be merged without being released. The workflow chapter in the Part on Git compares trunk-based development with Git Flow and GitHub Flow. A long-lived feature branch that is rebased on main every morning is not continuous integration, because the combined state is never built.

#### Measuring the result: DORA metrics

DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) is a research programme on software delivery performance. Its model defines five software delivery metrics in two groups. The definitions below are quoted in substance from the DORA website (per dora.dev, consulted October 2026).

blocks.caption: DORA software delivery metrics (per dora.dev, consulted October 2026).

blocks.text:
The site also states that the model evolved from the earlier "four keys", which used mean time to restore (MTTR) in place of failed deployment recovery time and did not include the rework rate. Older articles and interview questions use the four-key vocabulary, so both sets of names occur in practice. The metrics are diagnostic and not targets: if a team is rewarded for deployment frequency, trivial deployments inflate the number without improving delivery. They are read together, because a high deployment frequency with a high change fail rate indicates a pipeline that ships quickly without adequate verification.

### Worked example

#### Computing the metrics from a deployment log

The metrics are simple arithmetic over a deployment log. The following script computes four of them from a small CSV file. The data are synthetic and were invented for this example; a real team extracts the same fields from the deployment tool and the Git history (commit time of the oldest change in the deployment, deployment time, failure flag, time of recovery).

**deployments.csv (synthetic data)**

blocks.code:
import csv
import statistics
from datetime import datetime

FMT = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M"

with open("deployments.csv", newline="") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

lead_hours, recoveries = [], []
for r in rows:
    commit = datetime.strptime(r["commit_time"], FMT)
    deploy = datetime.strptime(r["deploy_time"], FMT)
    lead_hours.append((deploy - commit).total_seconds() / 3600)
    if r["failed"] == "yes":
        recovered = datetime.strptime(r["recovered_time"], FMT)
        recoveries.append((recovered - deploy).total_seconds() / 60)

first = datetime.strptime(rows[0]["deploy_time"], FMT)
last = datetime.strptime(rows[-1]["deploy_time"], FMT)
days = (last - first).total_seconds() / 86400

print("deployments:               ", len(rows))
print("period (days):              %.1f" % days)
print("deployments per week:       %.1f" % (len(rows) / days * 7))
print("median change lead time (h):%.2f" % statistics.median(lead_hours))
print("change fail rate:           %.0f%%" % (100 * len(recoveries) / len(rows)))
print("median recovery time (min): %.0f" % statistics.median(recoveries))

blocks.title: Run on the build machine (real output)

blocks.text:
Two observations follow from the data. The median lead time (1.58 hours) is much smaller than the mean, because the two deployments that waited overnight (d3 and d7, about 19 and 18 hours) are outliers; the median is therefore the more informative statistic for a skewed distribution. The change fail rate of 25 percent (two of eight deployments) is high, and both failures were recovered in 45 minutes, which indicates that rollback works but verification before deployment does not. Which metric to improve first depends on such a reading, not on the absolute values.

#### The pipeline of orders-service in neutral notation

Before any CI tool is chosen, the pipeline is specified in tool-independent form: the trigger, the stages, the command of each stage, the exit criterion and the artifact produced. The same specification is later realised as a GitHub Actions workflow (see the chapter on GitHub Actions fundamentals) and as a Jenkinsfile.

**pipeline-spec.txt**

blocks.code:
trigger:  every push to main; every pull request targeting main
runtime:  JDK 21, Maven 3.9 (via ./mvnw), PostgreSQL 16 for integration tests

stage 1  compile        ./mvnw -B compile                    stop on any compiler error
stage 2  unit-test      ./mvnw -B test                       stop on any test failure
stage 3  package        ./mvnw -B -DskipTests package        output: target/orders-service-X.jar
stage 4  integ-test     ./mvnw -B verify                     Failsafe tests against PostgreSQL
stage 5  publish        docker build + push, tag = Git SHA   output: image digest (main only)
stage 6  deploy-stage   deploy script, environment=staging   then: curl /actuator/health
stage 7  approve        human approval (continuous delivery) skipped for continuous deployment
stage 8  deploy-prod    same script, environment=production  then: curl /actuator/health

failure policy:  stop at first failing stage; notify the author of the commit
retention:       test reports 14 days; images keyed by SHA, kept per registry policy

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

The exercise establishes a baseline for the own project before any automation is written.

1. Write the stage list for the own Spring Boot project in the format of `pipeline-spec.txt`, with one real command per stage. A stage that has no command yet (for example static analysis) is marked as missing; the list of missing stages is the improvement backlog.
2. Measure the duration of the commit stage on the own machine: `time ./mvnw -B verify`. The value is a lower bound for the CI duration, because a CI runner starts with an empty dependency cache.
3. Measure the current change lead time from Git data. The command below prints the commit time and subject of the last ten commits as Unix timestamps; the difference between the commit time and the time the change was last deployed gives the lead time of that change.
4. List every manual step between a merged commit and a running release (copying a file, restarting a service, editing a setting). Each manual step is a candidate for automation, and the number of such steps is the main obstacle to continuous delivery.

blocks.code:
$ git log -n 3 --format='%h %ct %s'
ed94493 1791885600 Add order total validation
9c32ebb 1791799200 Extract OrderCalculator
0e40be3 1791712800 Initial order endpoint
blocks.title: Commit times as Unix timestamps (real output from a three-commit practice repository; hashes differ per repository)

blocks.text:
The format placeholders are `%h` (abbreviated hash), `%ct` (committer date as a Unix timestamp) and `%s` (subject).

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: the tested artifact differs from the deployed artifact

**Scenario.** The pipeline builds `orders-service` in a "build-staging" job and again in a separate "build-prod" job when the release is approved. Staging tests pass.

**Symptoms.** Production shows a `NoSuchMethodError` that never occurred in staging. The commit SHA is identical in both environments.

**Diagnosis.** The two jars are compared with `sha256sum`, and the checksums differ. Listing the embedded libraries of both jars with `unzip -l app.jar` and filtering for `BOOT-INF/lib` shows that one library appears in a newer version in the second build, because the `pom.xml` declares that dependency with a version range (or a snapshot version) that resolved differently at the time of each build.

**Root cause.** Two builds of one commit are not guaranteed to produce the same artifact when dependency resolution is not pinned, and the pipeline contains two builds.

**Fix.** Build once in the acceptance stage, publish the jar or image under a unique version, and deploy that artifact to every environment. Pin dependency versions (Spring Boot's dependency management already fixes most versions through the parent POM). **Prevention.** Reference artifacts by digest or immutable version in deployment jobs, never by branch name or `latest`. Add a check that fails when a deployment job contains a build command.

#### Problem: the mainline is red for days and everybody ignores it

**Scenario.** The CI build of `main` has failed intermittently for three weeks. Developers merge anyway, because "the failure is probably unrelated".

**Symptoms.** New failures hide among old ones. A defect that breaks the order total calculation is merged and detected only in staging.

**Diagnosis.** The CI history shows alternating red and green runs for the same commit, and a list of the failing test names shows that two tests fail in about one run of five (flaky tests, see the next chapter).

**Root cause.** The agreement that a red mainline is the top priority is not in force, and the failing build carries no consequence. The tool works, and the practice has been abandoned.

**Fix.** Revert or fix the breaking change immediately; quarantine genuinely flaky tests (move them to a separate, non-blocking job with a ticket and an owner) and restore a deterministic mainline. Enable branch protection with required status checks so that a pull request cannot merge with a red build (see the chapter on GitHub in the Part on Git).

**Prevention.** Track the share of red builds on the mainline as a team metric, and treat a build that is red for more than one working day as an incident.

### Questions to expect

1. **What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?** Both automate the path to a releasable artifact. In delivery, a human decides when to release the artifact that passed the pipeline; in deployment, every change that passes the pipeline is released automatically. Delivery is a prerequisite for deployment.
2. **What is continuous integration, and what does it require besides a CI server?** Frequent merging into a shared mainline, verified by an automated build and tests. It additionally requires short-lived branches, a fast test suite, and the team agreement to fix a broken mainline at once.
3. **Why should an artifact be built once?** The tested binary must be the deployed binary. Rebuilding per environment produces different artifacts for the same commit and invalidates the test results. Environments differ only by configuration injected at deployment time.
4. **What does "pipeline as code" mean, and what does it give?** The pipeline definition lives in the repository (a workflow YAML file or a Jenkinsfile). It gives history, code review, reproducibility for old commits and recovery after loss of the CI server.
5. **Name the DORA metrics.** Change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate. The first three measure throughput and the last two measure instability. Earlier material uses four keys with mean time to restore instead of recovery time and without the rework rate.
6. **Why are feature flags needed in trunk-based development?** They allow unfinished work to be merged and deployed in a disabled state, so integration stays continuous while release remains a separate decision.
7. **A pipeline takes 45 minutes. What is done?** Measure each stage, run independent jobs in parallel, cache dependencies, move slow tests to a later stage, run only affected tests where reliable, and fail fast by ordering cheap checks first.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Continuous integration means frequent merges to the mainline verified by automated build and tests; continuous delivery keeps every commit releasable with a manual release decision; continuous deployment removes that

decision.

- A pipeline is an ordered series of stages that answer one question each and stops at the first failure; cheap checks run first.
- Build once, publish an immutable artifact with a unique identifier, and promote it through environments that differ only in configuration.
- Pipeline definitions are stored as code in the repository, reviewed and versioned like source.
- DORA reports five metrics in two groups, throughput and instability; they are diagnostic and are read together.
- The practice fails when the team tolerates a red mainline, whatever tool is used.

sections.title: The Build and Test Pipeline for a Spring Boot Service

blocks.text:
The first half of every pipeline for a Java service is a Maven build: compile the code, run the tests, produce the jar. The CI server contributes a clean machine, a trigger and a place to store reports, and Maven contributes the build logic. A pipeline is therefore only as reliable as the Maven build that it invokes, and most pipeline failures that are blamed on "CI" are build problems that exist on every machine: a test that depends on the time zone, a test that is flaky, an integration test that is never executed, a dependency cache that is empty.

This chapter explains how the Maven lifecycle maps onto pipeline stages, how unit and integration tests are separated, how coverage is measured and enforced, how builds are made fast and reproducible, and how a pipeline can be simulated on a single machine with a shell script. The Spring Boot Maven basics (project structure, starters, the parent POM) are assumed from the Spring Boot guides and are not repeated.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Lifecycle, phases and goals

Maven (the build tool configured by a `pom.xml`, the Project Object Model) defines a build lifecycle as an ordered list of phases. A phase is a named step such as `compile` or `test`; it does no work itself. Work is done by goals, which are tasks provided by plugins, for example `compiler:compile` (the goal `compile` of the Maven Compiler Plugin). Each plugin goal is bound to a phase, either by default for the packaging type (`jar`) or by configuration in the `pom.xml`. Running a phase runs every earlier phase of the lifecycle first, in order. This rule is the most important property of the lifecycle for pipeline design: `mvn verify` includes compilation, unit tests, packaging and integration tests, and nothing needs to be run before it.

Phases without a default binding, such as `verify`, run but do nothing until a plugin binds a goal to them. The page recommends `mvn verify` when unsure which phase is needed; its effect is usually the same as `package`, but it also runs integration tests and checks bound to `verify`.

blocks.caption: Maven commands and the pipeline stage each one implements.

blocks.text:
For a service that is delivered as a container image, `mvn install` and `mvn deploy` are normally unnecessary: the artifact is the image, and the jar is an intermediate product. A common mistake is `mvn clean install` in CI, which adds a copy into the cache directory that nothing reads.

#### Unit tests and integration tests: Surefire and Failsafe

Two plugins run tests, and they differ in the phase and in the failure behaviour. The Surefire plugin runs unit tests in the `test` phase. The Failsafe plugin runs integration tests in the `integration-test` phase, and its separate `verify` goal evaluates the result in the `verify` phase. The split exists so that a failing integration test does not skip the `post-integration-test` phase, where services started in `pre-integration-test` are stopped. Per the plugin documentation (maven.apache.org/surefire, consulted October 2026), a build invoked as `mvn verify` runs the complete sequence, whereas `mvn integration-test` leaves `post-integration-test` unexecuted and is therefore not recommended.

The two plugins select test classes by name. Both lists below are quoted from the plugin documentation of the same date.

blocks.caption: Default test class name patterns.

blocks.text:
The naming is the whole mechanism. A class `OrderRepositoryIT` is skipped by Surefire and picked up by Failsafe, and a class `OrderRepositoryTests` runs in Surefire. Teams that name every Spring test `*Tests` (the Spring Initializr default is `OrdersServiceApplicationTests`) run all of them in the `test` phase, which is acceptable as long as the unit test stage does not need a database.

#### The test pyramid

Tests are not equal in cost. A unit test runs in milliseconds without Spring, a database or a network. An integration test starts part of the application or a real PostgreSQL (for example through Testcontainers, see the Spring Boot advanced guide) and takes seconds. An end-to-end test drives a deployed environment and takes minutes and is the most fragile. The test pyramid is the guideline that the number of tests should decrease up the pyramid.

blocks.text:
In Spring Boot terms, the base layer is plain JUnit 5 tests of services and domain classes with mocks (Mockito); the middle layer is `@WebMvcTest` (controller slice), `@DataJpaTest` (repository slice) and `@SpringBootTest` with a Testcontainers PostgreSQL; the top layer is a smoke test of the deployed service in staging. The slices and Testcontainers are covered in the Spring Boot material and are only placed on the pyramid here.

#### Reports and coverage with JaCoCo

A CI run must leave evidence. Surefire writes one XML file per test class to `target/surefire-reports/` (names `TEST-<class>.xml`), and Failsafe writes to `target/failsafe-reports/`. CI servers parse this JUnit XML format to display counts, failures and durations.

JaCoCo (Java Code Coverage) measures which code was executed during the tests. Its Maven plugin offers three relevant goals (per jacoco.org, Maven plugin documentation, consulted October 2026): `prepare-agent` attaches the JaCoCo runtime agent to the test JVM through the `argLine` property, `report` converts the recorded data (`target/jacoco.exec`) into an HTML and XML report under `target/site/jacoco/`, and `check` fails the build if rules are violated. A coverage number states how much code the tests executed, not how well it was verified: a test without assertions yields coverage and no protection. A threshold is useful as a ratchet that prevents decline, and harmful as a target to be gamed.

The following configuration is the build section of the `pom.xml` of `orders-service`. It is illustrative configuration (not run): Maven cannot download plugins on the build machine. The Spring Boot parent POM manages the versions of the Surefire, Failsafe and Spring Boot plugins, so only the JaCoCo plugin needs an explicit version. Version 0.8.15 is the latest release listed in the Maven Central metadata file of the plugin (consulted October 2026).

blocks.code:
<properties>
  <java.version>21</java.version>
  <jacoco.version>0.8.15</jacoco.version>
  <project.build.outputTimestamp>2026-01-01T00:00:00Z</project.build.outputTimestamp>
  <argLine></argLine>
</properties>

<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <goals>
            <goal>build-info</goal>
          </goals>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>

    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
      <configuration>
        <argLine>@{argLine} -Duser.timezone=UTC -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8</argLine>
      </configuration>
    </plugin>

    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
      <configuration>
        <argLine>@{argLine} -Duser.timezone=UTC -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8</argLine>
      </configuration>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <goals>
            <goal>integration-test</goal>
            <goal>verify</goal>
          </goals>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>

    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
      <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>${jacoco.version}</version>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <id>prepare-agent</id>
          <goals>
            <goal>prepare-agent</goal>
          </goals>
        </execution>
        <execution>
          <id>report</id>
          <phase>verify</phase>
          <goals>
            <goal>report</goal>
          </goals>
        </execution>
        <execution>
          <id>check</id>
          <phase>verify</phase>
          <goals>
            <goal>check</goal>
          </goals>
          <configuration>
            <rules>
              <rule>
                <element>BUNDLE</element>
                <limits>
                  <limit>
                    <counter>LINE</counter>
                    <value>COVEREDRATIO</value>
                    <minimum>0.70</minimum>
                  </limit>
                </limits>
              </rule>
            </rules>
          </configuration>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
blocks.title: pom.xml (build section, illustrative configuration, not run)

blocks.text:
Four details of this listing matter. The `<argLine>@{argLine} ...</argLine>` form uses late property evaluation (`@{...}`): JaCoCo's `prepare-agent` sets the `argLine` property to the agent option, and an `<argLine>` configured in Surefire with ordinary `${argLine}` syntax would be evaluated too early or would replace the agent option, which silently produces 0 percent coverage. The empty `<argLine></argLine>` property prevents an error when the property is not yet defined. The `-Duser.timezone=UTC` option removes dependence on the time zone of the machine (see the problem of a build that passes locally and fails in CI). The `report` execution is listed before `check`, because executions bound to the same phase run in POM order and the check reads the recorded data and not the report. The `<project.build.outputTimestamp>` property is explained in the section on reproducible builds.

#### Dependency caching

Maven stores downloaded plugins and dependencies in the local repository, by default `~/.m2/repository`. A new CI runner starts with an empty one, so the first Maven command downloads hundreds of megabytes. The following demonstration shows the effect on a build machine without network access and with an empty local repository (real output, trimmed and re-wrapped): Maven cannot resolve the plugin that the `compile` phase needs.

blocks.code:
$ mvn -o -B compile
[INFO] Scanning for projects...
[INFO] Building orders-core 1.0.0
[INFO] BUILD FAILURE
[ERROR] Plugin org.apache.maven.plugins:maven-resources-plugin:3.3.1 or one of its dependencies
[ERROR] could not be resolved: Cannot access central (https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2) in
[ERROR] offline mode and the artifact ...maven-resources-plugin:jar:3.3.1 has not been downloaded
blocks.title: Empty local repository, offline: plugin resolution fails (real output, trimmed)

blocks.text:
The remedy in CI is to restore `~/.m2/repository` from a cache at the start of the job and save it at the end. The cache key is derived from the content of `pom.xml` files, so that a change of dependencies produces a new cache and an unchanged POM reuses the old one. The chapters on GitHub Actions show the configuration; the mechanism is independent of the tool.

#### Maven wrapper

The Maven wrapper is a script pair (`mvnw` for Unix, `mvnw.cmd` for Windows) and a file `.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties` that names the Maven distribution to use (`distributionUrl`). When `./mvnw` runs, it downloads that Maven version if it is not present and then runs it (per maven.apache.org/wrapper, consulted October 2026). The wrapper makes the Maven version a property of the repository instead of the machine: a developer laptop with Maven 3.9.x and a CI runner with a different preinstalled version build with the same version. The wrapper files are created once with `mvn wrapper:wrapper` and committed; Spring Initializr projects already contain them. Optional properties `distributionSha256Sum` and `wrapperSha256Sum` verify the downloads against tampering.

#### Reproducible builds

A build is reproducible when building the same commit twice yields byte-identical artifacts. Reproducibility is a prerequisite for the claim that the tested artifact is the deployed artifact, and it allows independent verification of a release. The typical cause of a difference is a timestamp inside the jar. Maven documents the property `project.build.outputTimestamp`, which fixes the timestamp that plugins write into archives; since Maven 3.10.0 and 4.0.0-beta-5 reproducible mode is active by default (per maven.apache.org, guide to reproducible builds, consulted October 2026), and with older versions the property must be set. The Spring Boot Maven plugin honours the same property for the executable jar (per docs.spring.io, consulted October 2026). The same page lists other causes of differences: version ranges in dependencies, line endings, a different JDK major version, plugins that are not reproducible, and environment details such as the user name or the build path.

#### Profiles, versions and build metadata

A Maven profile is a named set of build configuration that is activated by `-P name`, an environment or a property. Profiles are useful for optional parts of the build (a profile `slow-tests`, a profile `sonar`). They are dangerous when they change what is built: if staging and production jars are produced with different profiles, the build-once rule is broken. Maven profiles are not Spring profiles; the latter select configuration at run time (`SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`) and do not affect the build.

The artifact version in the POM follows the release process: `1.4.0-SNAPSHOT` during development and `1.4.0` for a release. A snapshot is a moving target, so a deployment must never refer to one. For traceability the build records its origin: the Spring Boot goal `build-info` writes `META-INF/build-info.properties`, which the Actuator `info` endpoint exposes, and the Git commit SHA is added as an image tag and an OCI label (see the chapter on GitHub Actions advanced topics).

#### Command line options for CI

rows: Non-interactive; no colour, no download progress animation
Suppresses per-file download lines, which shortens the log considerably
Stop the multi-module build at the first failure (the default)
Continue with modules that do not depend on the failed one; shows more failures per run
One build thread per CPU core; parallel multi-module builds
Compile tests but do not run them
Build one module and the modules it depends on
blocks.caption: Maven options used in pipelines.

blocks.text:
Skipping tests in a pipeline is legitimate in exactly one situation: a later job builds an artifact from a commit whose tests have already passed in an earlier job. Using `-DskipTests` to make a red pipeline green is the practice that CI exists to prevent.

### Worked example

#### A pipeline simulated on one machine

A CI pipeline is a shell script with a policy: run the stages in order, stop at the first failure, keep the evidence. Maven plugins cannot be downloaded on the build machine, so the simulation uses `javac`, `java` and `jar` from the JDK directly and a deliberately small test harness. The stage names correspond to the Maven phases of the preceding figure. The domain class is the order total calculation of `orders-service`.

blocks.title: OrderCalculator.java
OrderCalculatorTest.java

blocks.text: The test class is a plain `main` program that exits with status 1 on failure; JUnit does the same job with annotations and reports, and a CI server decides only by the exit status. The pipeline script follows.

blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Local simulation of a CI pipeline: every stage must succeed or the script stops.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
OUT=target
stage() { printf '\n=== STAGE %s ===\n' "$1"; STAGE_START=$(date +%s%N); }
done_stage() {
  printf -- '--- %s finished in %d ms\n' "$1" $(( ($(date +%s%N) - STAGE_START) / 1000000 ))
}

stage validate
java -version 2>&1 | grep -v 'Picked up' | head -1
test -f src/main/java/com/example/orders/OrderCalculator.java
done_stage validate

stage compile
rm -rf "$OUT"; mkdir -p "$OUT/classes" "$OUT/test-classes"
javac -Xlint:all -d "$OUT/classes" $(find src/main -name '*.java')
echo "compiled $(find "$OUT/classes" -name '*.class' | wc -l) main classes"
done_stage compile

stage test
javac -d "$OUT/test-classes" -cp "$OUT/classes" $(find src/test -name '*.java')
java -cp "$OUT/classes:$OUT/test-classes" com.example.orders.OrderCalculatorTest
done_stage test

stage package
jar --create --file "$OUT/orders-core-1.0.0.jar" --date=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z -C "$OUT/classes" .
sha256sum "$OUT/orders-core-1.0.0.jar" | cut -c1-16
done_stage package

stage verify
jar --list --file "$OUT/orders-core-1.0.0.jar" | grep -c 'OrderCalculator' \
  | sed 's/^/classes in jar matching OrderCalculator: /'
done_stage verify
echo; echo "PIPELINE SUCCESS"
blocks.title: pipeline.sh

blocks.text: What to notice: `set -euo pipefail` makes the shell abort at the first command with a non-zero exit status (`-e`), at an unset variable (`-u`) and at a failure anywhere in a pipeline (`-o pipefail`); this is the same rule a CI server applies to every step. The `jar --date` option fixes the timestamps of the archive entries and is the JDK equivalent of `project.build.outputTimestamp`. A first run produces the following output; durations vary between runs and machines and are marked as measured on the build machine.

blocks.code:

=== STAGE package ===
3ce2e87445d8b70d

blocks.title: Failing run (real output)

blocks.text:
#### Reproducibility demonstrated

Two jars were built from the same classes with the command `jar --create`, first without a fixed date and two seconds apart, then with `--date=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z`. The first 16 hexadecimal digits of the SHA-256 checksums are shown.

blocks.code:
$ jar --create --file a.jar -C classes . ; sleep 2; jar --create --file b.jar -C classes .
$ sha256sum a.jar b.jar | cut -c1-16
003788808a6fbc63
d5e6f83eda164ddc
$ jar --create --file c.jar --date=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z -C classes .
$ jar --create --file d.jar --date=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z -C classes .
$ sha256sum c.jar d.jar | cut -c1-16
3ce2e87445d8b70d
3ce2e87445d8b70d
blocks.title: Archive checksums with and without a fixed timestamp (real output)

blocks.text:
The identical classes produce different archives because of the entry timestamps, and identical archives once the timestamp is fixed. The checksum `3ce2e87445d8b70d` also matched across the two complete pipeline runs, including a recompilation from source.

#### Maven on the build machine

Maven runs on the build machine; only downloads are impossible. `mvn -v` reports Apache Maven 3.9.11 with Java 21.0.12.1 (real output), and `mvn -o validate` on a POM without dependencies and plugins ends with `BUILD SUCCESS`, because the `validate` phase has no bound goal and needs no plugin.

### Hands-on

1. Copy the three files (`OrderCalculator.java`, `OrderCalculatorTest.java`, `pipeline.sh`) into a directory with the layout `src/main/java/com/example/orders/`, `src/test/java/com/example/orders/` and the script at the top level. Make the script executable with `chmod +x pipeline.sh` and run it. Expect `PIPELINE SUCCESS`.
2. Break the code as in the failing run (remove `.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(line.quantity()))`). Run the script again, read which stage failed, and print the exit status with `echo $?`.
3. Restore the code. Add a fourth check to the test class: a negative quantity must be rejected. Run the script and confirm that the new check passes without changing the production code, because `quantity() <= 0` already covers it.
4. Add a stage between `package` and `verify` that fails when the jar is larger than 10 kilobytes (`stat -c %s file`). A size budget is a simple quality gate of the same kind as a coverage threshold.
5. For a real Spring Boot project: run `./mvnw -B verify`, then open `target/site/jacoco/index.html` after adding the JaCoCo plugin from the listing, and find the class with the lowest coverage.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: a flaky test blocks the pipeline

**Scenario.** `OrderExpiryServiceTest` passes locally and in most CI runs, and fails in about one run of six. Developers press "re-run" until the build is green.

**Symptoms.** The failure message differs between runs or points at a timing assertion; a re-run of the same commit succeeds. The pipeline duration grows because of re-runs, and the team begins to distrust red builds.

**Diagnosis.** The test is executed repeatedly in a loop to estimate the failure rate and to reproduce the failure locally. The following experiment uses a program with a data race as a stand-in for a timing-dependent test: two threads increment an unsynchronised counter 2000 times each, and the test expects 4000.

blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
pass=0; fail=0
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  if java -cp . FlakyCounterTest | head -1 | grep -q PASS; then
    pass=$((pass+1))
  else
    fail=$((fail+1))
  fi
done
echo "pass=$pass fail=$fail"
blocks.title: repeat.sh

blocks.code:
$ bash repeat.sh
pass=17 fail=3
$ java -cp . FlakyCounterTest
FAIL counter=3968
blocks.title: Repeating a nondeterministic test 20 times (typical output; results vary between runs)

blocks.text:
A failure rate of 15 percent in a loop corresponds to the observed behaviour in CI. In a Maven project the equivalent loop is `for i in $(seq 1 30); do ./mvnw -q -Dtest=OrderExpiryServiceTest test || echo "failed run $i";` `done`.

**Root cause.** A test is flaky when its outcome depends on something the test does not control: thread scheduling, the wall clock, the order of tests, shared state in a database, the speed of the machine, an external service. In the example the cause is a data race in the code under test; in `OrderExpiryServiceTest` the cause was `Thread.sleep(100)` followed by an assertion on `Instant.now()`, which fails on a loaded CI runner.

**Fix.** Remove the uncontrolled input instead of retrying. Inject a `java.time.Clock` into the service and use a fixed clock in the test; replace sleeps by explicit waiting for a condition (a library such as Awaitility polls until a condition holds or a timeout expires); make shared state explicit and reset it for each test; fix real races in production code. As a stopgap, quarantine the test: tag it (`@Tag("flaky")`), exclude the tag from the blocking job (`-DexcludedGroups=flaky`) and run it in a separate non-blocking job with a ticket that has an owner.

**Prevention.** Automatic retries in the build (Surefire `rerunFailingTestsCount`) mark a test as flaky in the report but hide the defect when the setting is permanent; use them to measure flakiness, not to remove it. Track the number of re-runs per week as a team metric.

#### Problem: the build passes locally and fails in CI

**Scenario.** `InvoiceDateTest` asserts that an order created at 2026-10-19 20:00 UTC has the invoice date 2026-10-20. It passes on the laptop of a developer in India and fails in CI.

**Symptoms.** The assertion message shows an invoice date one day earlier in CI. Other typical symptoms of the same class: a `NoSuchMethodError` or `UnsupportedClassVersionError` (different JDK), file-name case differences (the CI file system is case-sensitive and the developer laptop is not), a missing environment variable, a test that depends on execution order.

**Diagnosis.** The CI log is compared with the local environment: JDK version (`java -version`), time zone, locale, file encoding. The program below reproduces the failure by running the same test in two zones through the `TZ` environment variable.

blocks.code:
$ TZ=Asia/Kolkata java -cp . InvoiceDateTest
PASS zone=Asia/Kolkata invoiceDate=2026-10-20
$ TZ=UTC java -cp . InvoiceDateTest
FAIL zone=UTC invoiceDate=2026-10-19
blocks.title: The same test in two time zones (real output)

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The code converts an `Instant` to a date with `ZoneId.systemDefault()`. The result depends on the time zone of the machine: a GitHub-hosted runner uses UTC, whereas the laptop uses India Standard Time (UTC+05:30). The test encodes the developer's zone as an implicit requirement.

**Fix.** Make the zone an explicit parameter of the code (`ZoneId` injected or part of the business rule) and pass it in the test. Fix the environment of the tests so that every machine behaves alike: `-Duser.timezone=UTC` in the `argLine` (see the POM listing), `-Dfile.encoding=UTF-8`, and the same JDK version through the Maven toolchain or the CI configuration. Pin the Maven version with the wrapper. **Prevention.** Run the test suite in the CI time zone before pushing (`TZ=UTC ./mvnw verify`), and let the CI define the JDK in one place that the developers also use (for example the `java.version` property and the `.sdkmanrc` or `.tool-versions` file).

#### Problem: integration tests exist but never run in CI

**Scenario.** `OrderRepositoryIT` verifies a native query against PostgreSQL. The query is broken by a refactoring, the pipeline is green, and the defect is found in staging.

**Symptoms.** The CI log shows `Tests run:` lines for unit test classes only, and no Failsafe section appears.

**Diagnosis.** The pipeline runs `./mvnw test`. The log is searched for `maven-failsafe-plugin`; it does not occur.

**Root cause.** Failsafe binds to the `integration-test` and `verify` phases, which come after `test`. A command that stops at `test` never reaches them. A second cause of the same symptom is a class name that matches neither plugin pattern (`OrderRepositoryIntegrationTest` ends in `Test` and runs in Surefire, where no database exists, while `OrderRepoCheck` runs nowhere).

**Fix.** Run `./mvnw -B verify` in the pipeline and use the Failsafe naming convention `*IT`. Add the Failsafe plugin with both goals, `integration-test` and `verify`, as in the listing; without the `verify` goal Failsafe records failures but the build does not fail.

**Prevention.** Assert in the pipeline that the integration tests ran: for example, count the files `target/failsafe-reports/TEST-*.xml` and fail when the count is zero.

### Questions to expect

1. **Explain the Maven lifecycle.** The lifecycle is an ordered list of phases (validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy, among others). Plugins bind goals to phases. Running a phase runs all preceding phases. `mvn verify` therefore compiles, tests, packages and runs integration tests.
2. **What is the difference between Surefire and Failsafe?** Surefire runs unit tests in the `test` phase and fails the build immediately. Failsafe runs integration tests in `integration-test` and fails in `verify`, so that `post-integration-test` cleanup still runs. Default name patterns differ: `*Test`, `*Tests`, `Test*`, `*TestCase` versus `IT*`, `*IT`, `*ITCase`.
3. **What is the difference between** `-DskipTests` **and** `-Dmaven.test.skip=true`**?** The first compiles the tests and does not run them; the second does not even compile them, so test classes are not available (for example to build a test-jar).
4. **What does the test pyramid recommend?** Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and a small number of end-to-end tests at the top, because cost and fragility increase upward.
5. **What does JaCoCo measure, and what are its limits?** It records which lines, branches and instructions were executed during the tests. It does not measure the quality of assertions. A threshold prevents regression but cannot ensure good tests.
6. **Why does Maven take long on a fresh CI runner, and what helps?** The local repository `~/.m2` is empty, so plugins and dependencies are downloaded. Caching `~/.m2/repository` keyed by a hash of the `pom.xml` files restores it.
7. **What is a reproducible build, and how is it enabled in Maven?** Two builds of one commit produce identical bytes. Setting `project.build.outputTimestamp` (default behaviour from Maven 3.10.0), pinning plugin and dependency versions and using one JDK major version achieve it.
8. **A test fails only in CI. List the first checks.** JDK version, time zone, locale and encoding, case-sensitive file names, missing environment variables, dependence on test order or shared state, resources (memory, CPU) of the runner, and external services that are not reachable from the runner.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Maven phases are a fixed sequence; running a phase runs all earlier ones; `mvn verify` is the standard CI command because it includes integration tests and checks.
- Surefire runs unit tests by name pattern in `test`; Failsafe runs `*IT` classes in `integration-test` and evaluates them in `verify`; a pipeline that stops at `test` never runs them.
- Coverage tools measure executed code, not verified behaviour; use a threshold as a ratchet. With JaCoCo, use `@{argLine}` in Surefire and Failsafe to keep the agent.
- A flaky test is a defect: remove the uncontrolled input (clock, sleep, shared state), and quarantine only as a short-term measure.
- Make environments identical: wrapper for the Maven version, one JDK, UTC time zone and UTF-8 encoding set in the build, dependency cache for speed.
- A pipeline can be simulated by a script with `set -euo pipefail`; the contract is the same: stages in order and a non-zero exit status stops the run.

A pipeline definition is useful only when something executes it. A CI server has to notice a push, find a machine, check out the code, run the commands, store the results and report the status back to the pull request. Running such a server (patching it, scaling its build machines, wiring it to the repository) is itself a task that consumes time. GitHub Actions removes that task for projects hosted on GitHub: it is a CI/CD service built into GitHub, in which pipelines are YAML files stored in the repository and executed on machines provided by GitHub or by the project.

This chapter describes the building blocks of GitHub Actions (workflows, events, jobs, steps, actions, runners), the expression language and contexts, secrets and the `GITHUB_TOKEN`, concurrency control and service containers, and then assembles a complete `ci.yml` for `orders-service`. GitHub Actions cannot be run on the build machine that produced this book, since it requires GitHub itself. All workflow listings are therefore labelled illustrative configuration (not run). Each YAML listing was checked for syntax with PyYAML (`yaml.safe_load`), and the syntax and behaviour statements were checked against docs.github.com, consulted October 2026. Action versions were checked against the README files of the action repositories in the same month; versions change, and the Dependabot configuration in the next chapter keeps them current.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Vocabulary

rows: A YAML file in `.github/workflows/` that defines an automated process; a repository may contain many
Something that starts a workflow: a push, a pull request, a manual request, a schedule, a release
A set of steps that run on one runner; jobs of a workflow run in parallel unless ordered with `needs`
One unit of work in a job: either a shell command (`run`) or an action (`uses`); steps run sequentially
A reusable unit of work, referenced by `owner/repo@version`, for example `actions/checkout@v7`
The machine that executes a job: a GitHub-hosted virtual machine or a self-hosted machine
A file or directory stored by a workflow run and available for download or for later jobs
A named object (`github`, `env`, `secrets`, `matrix`, `needs`) read through expressions
Text inside `${{ }}` evaluated by GitHub before the step runs
blocks.caption: The terms of GitHub Actions.

blocks.text: The containment is: a workflow contains jobs, a job contains steps, and every job is assigned to one runner, which is a fresh machine for GitHub-hosted runners. Steps of one job share the runner file system and environment variables set with `GITHUB_ENV`, whereas two jobs share nothing except what is passed through outputs, artifacts or caches.

*command; jobs are connected only by* `needs`*, outputs and artifacts.*

#### From event to status check

When a push or pull request event occurs, GitHub searches the workflow files of the relevant commit and starts one run for every workflow whose `on:` filters match. Each job is queued until a runner with the requested label is free; the runner clones the repository at the commit, executes the steps and streams the log. On completion, the result is attached to the commit (and to the pull request) as a check. Branch protection rules can require specific checks to pass before merging (see the chapter on GitHub in the Part on Git).

blocks.text:
#### Events and trigger filters

The `on:` key lists the events that start the workflow. The most important ones are described in the table (per docs.github.com, events that trigger workflows, consulted October 2026).

rows: Runs when commits or tags are pushed, including branches not yet merged. Filters: `branches`, `tags`, `paths` (and their `-ignore` forms)

Default activity types are `opened`, `synchronize` and `reopened`. `GITHUB_SHA` is the last merge commit of the pull request (`refs/pull/N/merge`), not the branch head. The workflow does not run while the pull request has a merge conflict
Manual start from the web interface, the API or `gh workflow run`; may declare typed inputs (`string`, `boolean`, `choice`, `number`, `environment`)
Cron expression in UTC by default; runs on the default branch
Release lifecycle events (`published`, `created`, `released` and others); `GITHUB_REF` is `refs/tags/TAG`
Marks a reusable workflow that other workflows call (see the next chapter)
blocks.caption: Common events.

blocks.code:
on:
  push:
    branches: [main, "release/**"]
    tags: ["v*"]
    paths: ["src/**", "pom.xml"]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        description: Target environment
        type: choice
        options: [staging, production]
        default: staging
      skip_tests:
        type: boolean
        default: false
  schedule:
    - cron: "30 2 * * 1-5"
  release:
    types: [published]
blocks.title: trigger-examples.yml (illustrative configuration, not run)

blocks.text:
The filter rules are a frequent source of silent non-execution (per the workflow syntax reference, consulted October 2026). If only `tags` is defined for `push`, the workflow does not run for branch pushes, and if only `branches` is defined, it does not run for tags. When `branches` and `paths` are both present, both must match. Path filters are not evaluated for pushes of tags, so a tag push ignores `paths`. The positive and negative variants of one filter cannot be mixed (`branches` with `branches-ignore`), but `!` patterns inside `branches` exclude refs, and the order of patterns matters. A push with more than 1,000 commits always runs the workflow.

The five fields of a cron expression are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. The example `30 2 * * 1-5` means 02:30 UTC on Monday to Friday. The reference states that the shortest interval is five minutes and that scheduled runs use the workflow file on the default branch. The reference also documents an optional IANA `timezone` key for `schedule`; without it, cron times are UTC. Scheduled runs can be delayed under load and are not suitable for exact timing.

#### Jobs, dependencies and conditions

Jobs run in parallel by default. The `needs` key orders them: a job starts after the listed jobs succeeded, and is skipped if a dependency failed or was skipped, unless an `if` condition with a status check function overrides this. A job can publish values to dependent jobs through `outputs`, which are mapped from step outputs; a step writes an output by appending `name=value` to the file whose path is in `GITHUB_OUTPUT` (per docs.github.com, workflow commands, consulted October 2026).

blocks.code:
jobs:
  version:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      short_sha: ${{ steps.vars.outputs.short_sha }}
    steps:
      - id: vars
        run: echo "short_sha=${GITHUB_SHA::7}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
  use:
    needs: version
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Building ${{ needs.version.outputs.short_sha }}"
blocks.title: job-outputs.yml (illustrative configuration, not run)

blocks.text:
Output values are limited to 1 MB per job and 50 MB per workflow run, and outputs that contain a secret are redacted. The `if` key accepts an expression; the `${{ }}` delimiters are optional in `if` except when the expression starts with `!`, in which case they are required (a YAML syntax reason, since `!` introduces a tag). The status functions are `success()` (the default), `failure()`, `cancelled()` and `always()`. The documentation recommends `!cancelled()` over `always()` for steps that should run after failures, because `always()` also runs when the workflow was cancelled and can leave the run hanging.

#### Runners

A runner is the machine on which a job executes. Two kinds exist. A GitHub-hosted runner is a fresh virtual machine started for one job and discarded afterwards, with a software image maintained by GitHub. A self-hosted runner is a machine operated by the project or organisation, with the runner application installed and registered; it is free of GitHub charges but is the operator's responsibility (security, patching, capacity). The label in `runs-on` selects the kind and the image.

*Standard GitHub-hosted runner for the label ubuntu-latest (per docs.github.com, consulted October 2026).*

The label `ubuntu-latest` currently maps to Ubuntu 24.04 (per github.com/actions/runner-images, consulted October 2026). The documentation states that `-latest` labels can move to a newer operating system image over time, and recommends pinning an explicit label such as `ubuntu-24.04` when an unexpected image change is not acceptable. The 14 GB of storage is a limit that large builds can reach (see the problem on runner disk space in the next chapter).

#### uses and run

A step either runs a shell command or invokes an action. `run` executes its text in a shell; on Linux, when no shell is specified, the command line is `bash -e {0}`, and with an explicit `shell: bash` it is `bash --noprofile --norc -eo` `pipefail {0}` (per the workflow syntax reference). The difference is significant: only the explicit form fails when a command in the middle of a pipeline fails. `uses` references an action in the form `owner/repo@ref` (a tag, a branch or a commit SHA), a local path such as `./.github/actions/name`, or a container image. Actions are programs (JavaScript, Docker or composite) that read inputs given under `with:` and may produce outputs.

The `ref` after `@` decides how much trust is placed in the action's author. A version tag such as `v7` is a moving pointer that the author can re-point; a full-length commit SHA is immutable. GitHub's secure use reference advises pinning actions to a full-length commit SHA (consulted October 2026), and the next chapter shows how Dependabot updates pinned versions.

#### Contexts and expressions

An expression is written `${{ expression }}` and evaluated on the GitHub side before the step runs, which means the resulting text is substituted into the YAML value, including into `run` scripts. The expression reads contexts, which are objects with properties (per docs.github.com, contexts, consulted October 2026).

rows: Commit SHA that triggered the run (for pull requests, the merge commit)
Full ref such as `refs/heads/main`, and the short name `main`
User or app that initiated the run
Unique run identifier (unchanged on re-run), and per-workflow counter
Source branch of a pull request (empty for other events)
Workflow variables, and configuration variables at repository, organisation or environment level
Outputs of an earlier step, and of a direct dependency job
Values of the current matrix combination
blocks.caption: Frequently used contexts and properties.

blocks.text:
Functions are available in expressions: `contains`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `format`, `join`, `toJSON`, `fromJSON` and `hashFiles` (a SHA-256 hash over the files matching a glob, used for cache keys). Strings in expressions use single quotes; double quotes are a syntax error. Comparisons of strings ignore case. A reference to a property that does not exist evaluates to an empty string and does not fail, which hides typos in context names.

#### Environment variables, secrets and configuration variables

Variables are set with `env:` at workflow, job or step level; the most specific level wins, and values cannot refer to other keys of the same `env` map. GitHub sets default variables for every step, among them `GITHUB_SHA`, `GITHUB_REF`, `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, `GITHUB_RUN_ID`, `GITHUB_ACTOR`, `GITHUB_WORKSPACE`, `RUNNER_OS` and `CI=true`. Variables with the prefixes `GITHUB_` and `RUNNER_` cannot be overwritten (per docs.github.com, variables, consulted October 2026). A step can define a variable for later steps by appending `NAME=value` to the file named by `GITHUB_ENV`; the step that writes it does not see it.

Secrets are encrypted values stored at repository, environment or organisation level and read through `${{` `secrets.NAME }}`. Several rules follow from the documentation (consulted October 2026). Secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forks, except `GITHUB_TOKEN`; they are not passed automatically to reusable workflows; and they are not available to workflows triggered by Dependabot events. A secret cannot be referenced directly in an `if` condition; the workaround is to copy it into a job-level environment variable and test that. A secret that has not been set evaluates to an empty string. The size limit is 48 KB per secret. Secrets that are not stored in GitHub but are produced during the run can be registered for masking with the workflow command `::add-mask::VALUE`.

Secrets are redacted in logs by string match. The secure use reference states that redaction is not guaranteed: structured data such as JSON can defeat it, and values derived from a secret (base64 or URL-encoded forms) must be registered separately. A secret that appears in a log is treated as leaked, the log is deleted, and the secret is rotated.

Configuration variables (`vars`) hold non-sensitive settings such as a registry host name or a Java version. The most specific level wins: an environment variable overrides a repository variable, which overrides an organisation variable.

#### The GITHUB_TOKEN and permissions

At the start of each job GitHub creates a token, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, that allows the workflow to call the GitHub API on its own repository: to comment on a pull request, to push a package, to create a release. The token expires when the job ends (on GitHub-hosted runners at most after six hours) and is read as `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` or `${{ github.token` `}}`. Its permissions are controlled by the `permissions` key at workflow or job level. Setting any single scope sets every unlisted scope to `none`, and `permissions: {}` removes all access. The scopes include `contents`, `packages`, `pull-requests`, `issues`, `checks`, `statuses`, `deployments`, `actions` and `id-token`, among others, each with values `read`, `write` or `none`.

The default permissions depend on repository or organisation settings. According to the repository settings documentation (consulted October 2026), the restricted default grants read access to `contents` and `packages`, and the permissive default grants read and write to all scopes; new repositories in a personal account use the restricted default, and repositories in an organisation inherit the organisation's setting. A pipeline should not rely on the default: declaring `permissions: contents: read` at the top of every workflow and raising individual jobs only where needed is the least-privilege practice that the secure use reference recommends. Events caused by `GITHUB_TOKEN` generally do not start new workflow runs, which prevents recursive runs. The exceptions are `workflow_dispatch` and `repository_dispatch`. A commit pushed with the token therefore does not trigger a `push` workflow, and a tag created with it does not trigger a release workflow (see the problem of a tag that does not trigger the release workflow in the next chapter).

blocks.text:
The fork rule exists because the pull request code is written by someone who has no write access. If the workflow could read secrets when running a fork's code, the contributor could add a line that prints the secrets. For forks, events go to the base repository, secrets are not passed except the read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and (by default) a maintainer must approve the first run of a first-time contributor. The event `pull_request_target` runs the workflow definition from the base branch with access to secrets and is for that reason dangerous: the secure use reference advises avoiding it unless necessary and never checking out and executing the pull request code within it.

#### Concurrency

Pushing three commits within a minute starts three runs of the same workflow, and only the last one is of interest. The `concurrency` key defines a group; only one run of a group executes at a time, and `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels a running run when a newer one enters the group. A group name is a string or an expression and is case-insensitive. By default, one pending run is kept and further pending runs are replaced.

blocks.text:
The group name must separate unrelated runs. A group `ci-${{ github.ref }}` separates branches, and the expression `${{ github.head_ref || github.ref }}` handles pull requests (where `head_ref` is set) and pushes (where it is empty) with one rule. Cancelling in-progress runs is appropriate for CI on branches and inappropriate for deployments to production, where an interrupted deployment may leave the environment in an undefined state; deployment workflows use a group without cancellation so that runs queue.

#### Service containers

An integration test needs a PostgreSQL instance. A service container is a Docker container that GitHub starts for the duration of the job, defined under `services:`. When the job runs directly on the runner machine, the container's port is mapped to the machine with `ports:` and reached at `localhost`; when the job itself runs in a container, both are placed in one user-defined Docker network, no port mapping is needed, and the service label (here `postgres`) is the host name (per docs.github.com, PostgreSQL service containers, consulted October 2026). The `options` field passes flags to `docker create`; a `--health-cmd` makes the job wait until the database accepts connections, which avoids the race between container start and the first connection.

blocks.text:
### Worked example

#### The complete ci.yml for orders-service

The workflow below builds and verifies `orders-service` on every pull request to `main` and every push to `main`, runs the integration tests against a PostgreSQL service container, and keeps the test reports. It is illustrative configuration (not run). The password `ci-only-password` protects a throwaway database that exists for the duration of one job and has no network exposure; it is deliberately not a secret, and no production credential belongs in a workflow file.

blocks.code:
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths-ignore:
      - "docs/**"
      - "**.md"
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.head_ref || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
build:
  name: Build and verify
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  timeout-minutes: 15
  services:
    postgres:
      image: postgres:16
      env:
        POSTGRES_DB: orders
        POSTGRES_USER: orders_app
        POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ci-only-password
      ports:
        - 5432:5432
      options: >-
        --health-cmd "pg_isready -U orders_app -d orders"
        --health-interval 5s
        --health-timeout 5s
        --health-retries 10
  steps:
    - name: Check out the commit
      uses: actions/checkout@v7

    - name: Set up JDK 21 with Maven cache
      uses: actions/setup-java@v6
      with:
        distribution: temurin
        java-version: "21"
        cache: maven

    - name: Build, test and verify
      run: ./mvnw --batch-mode --no-transfer-progress verify
      env:
        SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
        SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: orders_app
        SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ci-only-password

    - name: Upload test reports
      if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
      with:
        name: test-reports
        path: |
          target/surefire-reports/
          target/failsafe-reports/
          target/site/jacoco/
        retention-days: 14
        if-no-files-found: warn

summary:
  name: Report summary
  needs: build
  if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - name: Download test reports
      uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
      with:
        name: test-reports
        path: reports

    - name: Write job summary
      run: |
        {
          echo "## Test reports"
          echo "Result files: $(find reports -name 'TEST-*.xml' | wc -l)"
          echo "Build result: ${{ needs.build.result }}"
        } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
blocks.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml (illustrative configuration, not run)

blocks.text:
**job: build**

checkout

**service container**

setup-java 21 Maven cache postgres:16 push to main db: orders or pull request **reached at localhost:5432** **mvn -B verify**

upload test reports job: report and jar needs: build, if: always() runs even when build fails

*artifact: test-reports (XML)*

*Figure 3.14. The workflow has two jobs:* `build` *runs the Maven build next to a PostgreSQL service container and uploads the reports,* *and* `summary` *waits for it and runs even when* `build` *failed.*

#### Reading the file line by line

**Trigger and filters.** The `push` trigger is limited to `main` and ignores changes that touch only documentation (`paths-ignore`). The `pull_request` trigger has no path filter on purpose: a required status check whose workflow is skipped by a path filter stays "pending" forever, and the pull request cannot be merged (see the problem of a workflow that does not start, below). `workflow_dispatch` adds a manual "Run workflow" button.

**Permissions and concurrency.** `contents: read` gives the token the minimum needed by `actions/checkout`. The concurrency group contains the workflow name and either the pull request branch or the ref, so a new push to the same pull request cancels the previous run.

**The** `build` **job.** `timeout-minutes: 15` stops a hung build; the default is 360 minutes, which would consume a large part of the monthly allowance. `actions/checkout@v7` clones the commit. `actions/setup-java@v6` installs a Temurin JDK 21 (the `distribution` keyword `temurin` is one of the keywords documented in the action's README) and, with `cache: maven`, restores and saves `~/.m2` keyed by the hash of the POM files, as described in the preceding chapter. The Maven step runs `./mvnw` (the wrapper) with `verify`, so the integration tests run. Spring Boot reads `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL`, `SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME` and `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD` from the environment through relaxed binding, so the test configuration needs no change for CI.

**Uploading reports.** The condition `${{ !cancelled() }}` makes the step run after a failed Maven step (the default condition `success()` would skip it, and the failing reports would be lost) but not when the run was cancelled. The upload action's inputs `name`, `path`, `retention-days` (1 to 90, default 90) and `if-no-files-found` (`error`, `warn` or `ignore`) are documented in its README. Artifacts created with `upload-artifact` version 4 or later are immutable, and two jobs cannot upload to the same artifact name; matrix jobs therefore need unique names.

**The** `summary` **job.** `needs: build` orders it after `build`. The `!cancelled()` condition makes it run also when `build` failed, and the expression `${{ needs.build.result }}` contains `success`, `failure`, `cancelled` or `skipped`. The job downloads the artifact (the `name` input of `download-artifact@v8`; without it all artifacts are downloaded) and appends Markdown to the file named by `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`, which GitHub renders on the summary page of the run.

#### Validating the file

A YAML file is checked for syntax before it is committed, because a syntax error produces an invalid workflow that shows up as an error in the Actions tab instead of running. PyYAML parses the file, and a short script prints the structure that GitHub will see. Syntax validity is necessary and not sufficient: PyYAML does not know the workflow schema, so a misspelled key such as `runs_on` passes. A schema-aware linter (the third-party tool `actionlint` is widely used for this; it was not available on the build machine) or the GitHub editor detects such errors.

blocks.code:
import sys
import yaml

doc = yaml.safe_load(open(sys.argv[1]))
print("yaml.safe_load OK:", sys.argv[1])
print("top-level keys:", list(doc.keys()))
for name, job in doc["jobs"].items():
    steps = job.get("steps", [])
    kinds = ["uses" if "uses" in s else "run" for s in steps]
    print("job %-8s runs-on=%s needs=%s steps=%d (%s)"
          % (name, job.get("runs-on"), job.get("needs"), len(steps), ",".join(kinds)))
