blocks.caption: Contents of JENKINS_HOME and their role in backup: configuration and job definitions must be backed up, build records grow without bound and need pruning, and the secrets directory must be protected and stored separately.
blocks.alt: JENKINS_HOME (/var/lib/jenkins for the Linux package, /var/jenkins_home in the official image) | config.xml global settings, security realm back up | jobs/<name>/config.xml job definitions back up | jobs/<name>/builds/<n>/ console log, JUnit results, program.dat prune | secrets/ master.key and keys that decrypt credentials store separately | credentials.xml encrypted credential records back up | plugins/ installed plugin files (.jpi) rebuildable | workspace/ checkouts of builds run on the controller disposable | nodes/, users/ agent definitions, user accounts back up

blocks.text:
The jenkins.io page on backups states that backing up the entire directory preserves the whole controller and that restoring is a copy to the new system. It lists what can be excluded: checked-out sources under `workspace`, and the `war`, `cache` and `tools` directories, which are recreated. It also states that the controller key `master.key` must not be included in a regular backup and is to be stored separately in a very secure location, because it is needed for a full restore. The page recommends filesystem snapshots for consistency, notes that thinBackup is the only open-source backup plugin currently maintained, and recommends validating backups by restoring to a temporary directory and starting Jenkins on a different HTTP port.

#### Releases and Java versions

Jenkins publishes weekly releases and Long-Term Support (LTS) releases. The jenkins.io LTS page describes the cadence: every 12 weeks the community selects a recent release as the next baseline, and each baseline receives three LTS releases (X.1, X.2, X.3), each preceded by a release candidate two weeks earlier. A production controller normally follows LTS. Per the Jenkins changelog consulted in October 2026, the most recent LTS listed is 2.580.1 (30 September 2026), and the changelog states that Java 21 or Java 25 is required from LTS 2.555.1 onward and that Java 17 is not supported from that release. The Java support policy page lists Java 21 with planned end of support in September 2027 and Java 25 with planned end of support in September 2029. The version numbers above will be outdated when this text is read; the pages https://www.jenkins.io/download/lts/ and https://www.jenkins.io/changelog-stable/ are the sources to consult before an installation.

#### Security basics

Four mechanisms form the minimum security configuration, and all four are described in the jenkins.io security documentation.

1. **Authentication (security realm).** Jenkins' own user database is the default. Larger organizations connect LDAP or Active Directory, or single sign-on through SAML or OIDC plugins.
2. **Authorization.** The documentation advises against "Anyone can do anything" and "Legacy mode" for anything other than a local test controller. Matrix-based security assigns permissions per user and per group and is recommended as the starting point for production; it requires the Matrix Authorization Strategy plugin. Project-based matrix adds a permission list per project. Permissions are cumulative across the user, the user's groups and the "authenticated" and "anonymous" entries. The Role-based Authorization Strategy plugin supports role schemes.
3. **Credentials store.** Credentials are stored encrypted on the controller and referenced in pipelines only by ID. The Credentials Binding plugin supports secret text, username and password, secret file, SSH username with private key, certificate and Docker host certificate types. Masking of values in the console log reduces accidental exposure only, and the documentation warns against allowing untrusted pipelines to use trusted credentials.
4. **Isolation of builds from the controller.** Zero executors on the built-in node, agents with the minimum network access needed, and no inbound agent TCP port unless required.

### Worked example

The following sequence installs a controller from the official container image and connects one inbound agent. The commands follow the jenkins.io Docker installation page (consulted October 2026); the output is representative and was not produced on the build machine.

blocks.code:
$ docker run --name jenkins --restart=on-failure --detach \
    --publish 8080:8080 --publish 50000:50000 \
    --volume jenkins-data:/var/jenkins_home \
    jenkins/jenkins:lts-jdk21
3f0c9d2a41b7e0a8c6d5b1f27a9e4c3d8b6a5f10e2c7d9b4a1f3e6c8d0b2a579
$ docker logs jenkins 2>&1 | grep -A3 "initial setup"
Jenkins initial setup is required. An admin user has been created and a password generated.
Please use the following password to proceed to installation:

a8b1f0c2d3e44f5a9b6c7d8e9f0a1b2c
blocks.title: Start a Jenkins LTS controller in Docker (typical output, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
Port 8080 serves the web interface and port 50000 serves inbound TCP agents (the page notes both). The named volume `jenkins-data` keeps `JENKINS_HOME` when the container is replaced, which is what makes an upgrade a matter of starting a newer image against the same volume.

The setup wizard in the browser at `http://localhost:8080` asks for the initial administrator password (also at `/var/jenkins_home/secrets/initialAdminPassword`), offers to install a suggested set of plugins and then asks for the first administrator account. After the wizard, the following steps prepare the controller for `orders-service`.

1. Under **Manage Jenkins \> Nodes**, open the built-in node and set the number of executors to 0.
2. Create a permanent agent named `maven-agent-1` with remote root directory `/home/jenkins/agent`, label `maven-jdk21`, launch method "Launch agent by connecting it to the controller".
3. On the agent host (with JDK 21, Maven and Git installed), run the command shown on the node's status page. Its general form is the following (flag names from memory, verify before use against the page shown by the controller).

blocks.code:
$ java -jar agent.jar -url http://jenkins.example.com:8080/ \
    -secret 7c1e...redacted -name maven-agent-1 \
    -webSocket -workDir /home/jenkins/agent
INFO: Using /home/jenkins/agent/remoting as a remoting work directory
INFO: Connected
blocks.title: Start the inbound agent on the agent host (illustrative, not run)

blocks.text:
1. Create a Pipeline job from the repository containing the `Jenkinsfile` of `orders-service` (the file is developed in the next chapter) and start a build. The build appears in the queue, is assigned to `maven-agent-1` because of the label, and runs.

The same controller can be described as code with the Configuration as Code plugin (JCasC), so that the setup above is reproducible. JCasC reads YAML from the location named by the `CASC_JENKINS_CONFIG` variable (a folder, a file or a URL) and applies it at startup, according to the jenkins.io page on the plugin. The file has the top-level sections `jenkins`, `tool`, `unclassified` and `credentials`.

blocks.code:
jenkins:
  systemMessage: "orders-service CI, managed by Configuration as Code"
  numExecutors: 0
  securityRealm:
    local:
      allowsSignup: false
      users:
        - id: "admin"
          password: "${ADMIN_PASSWORD}"
  authorizationStrategy:
    globalMatrix:
      entries:
        - user:
            name: "admin"
            permissions:
              - "Overall/Administer"
        - group:
            name: "authenticated"
            permissions:
              - "Overall/Read"
              - "Job/Read"
              - "Job/Build"
  nodes:
    - permanent:
        name: "maven-agent-1"
        remoteFS: "/home/jenkins/agent"
        numExecutors: 2
        labelString: "maven-jdk21"
        launcher:
          inbound:
            workDirSettings:
              disabled: false
              internalDir: "remoting"
              failIfWorkDirIsMissing: false
unclassified:
  location:
    url: "https://jenkins.example.com/"
credentials:
  system:
    domainCredentials:
      - credentials:
          - usernamePassword:
              scope: GLOBAL
              id: "ghcr-push"
              username: "ci-bot"
              password: "${GHCR_TOKEN}"
blocks.title: jenkins.yaml (illustrative configuration, not run; YAML syntax checked with PyYAML)

blocks.text:
The YAML parses as valid YAML (`yaml.safe_load` succeeded on the build machine). The plugin's own schema, in particular the `globalMatrix` entry layout and the `inbound` launcher keys, was not validated, because the plugin could not be installed; the reference page generated by the running controller (**Manage Jenkins \> Configuration as Code** **\> Documentation**) is the authority. The jenkins.io page states that the plugin does not cover secret handling and that the `credentials` section may be deleted from the file. The example therefore uses `${GHCR_TOKEN}` placeholders that JCasC resolves from environment variables, so that no secret is written into the repository that holds the file.

### Hands-on

Objective: observe label matching, the queue and the effect of zero executors on the built-in node. A laptop with Docker and a second terminal are sufficient.

1. Start the controller with the `docker run` command above and complete the setup wizard.
2. Create a Freestyle job named `whoami` with the single build step "Execute shell": `hostname; echo "executors:` `$EXECUTOR_NUMBER"`. Run it. The console output shows the container's host name, because the build ran on the built-in node.
3. Set the built-in node to 0 executors and run the job again. The build now stays in the queue. The queue entry shows a message such as "Waiting for next available executor".
4. Create an inbound agent with the label `maven-jdk21` (a second container or a local `java -jar agent.jar` command works). Restrict the job to that label under "Restrict where this project can be run". The queued build starts as soon as the agent connects.
5. Stop the agent and start another build. Record the message shown in the queue. This is the signature of a missing agent and the first symptom in the first problem below.

Expected result: step 3 produces a build that never starts; step 4 starts it; the console output of step 4 shows the agent's host name rather than the controller's.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: an agent goes offline and builds wait

**Scenario.** Builds of `orders-service` begin to take over an hour to start. Only `maven-agent-1` carries the label `maven-jdk21`.

**Symptoms.** The queue shows builds with the reason "Waiting for next available executor" or "There are no nodes with the label". The agent appears with a red icon on the **Nodes** page.

**Diagnosis.** The node page shows why it is offline: a disconnected inbound agent (process stopped), a failed SSH launch (the log on the node page shows the exception), or a node taken offline by the monitors for low disk space or temp space. On the agent host, `systemctl status` of the service running `agent.jar` and `df -h` give the second half of the answer.

**Root cause.** In the typical case the agent host ran out of disk because workspaces and Maven repositories accumulated, Jenkins' disk-space monitor took the node offline, and no second agent carried the label.

**Fix.** Free space (delete old workspaces, `docker system prune` on that agent only after checking nothing else uses it), then bring the node back online from its page. Restart the agent service if the process had stopped.

**Prevention.** At least two agents per label, so that one failure reduces capacity rather than stopping the line. Workspace cleanup in the pipeline (`cleanWs()` in a `post` block) and a periodic cleanup job. Ephemeral agents remove this failure class entirely.

#### Problem 2: a plugin upgrade breaks pipelines

**Scenario.** After the weekly plugin update, every build fails at the first stage with an error from a Pipeline step that worked the day before.

**Symptoms.** Console output ends with an exception naming a plugin class or a missing step (`No such DSL method`), or the controller logs a plugin loading failure at start.

**Diagnosis.** The **Manage Jenkins \> Plugins \> Installed** page lists plugin versions; comparing with the previous state (the `.jpi` files in the backup, or the plugin list recorded in version control) identifies the update. The system log shows plugin load errors and missing dependencies.

**Root cause.** A plugin update changed behaviour or required a newer version of a dependent plugin, and several plugins were updated together without testing against the real pipelines. Plugins share the controller JVM, so an incompatibility is controller-wide.

**Fix.** Roll back by restoring the previous plugin files from backup (the jenkins.io page notes that older versions can be installed by copying a `.jpi` file into `JENKINS_HOME/plugins`, with a restart), then update one plugin at a time.

**Prevention.** Record the plugin list in version control (the container image build with a plugin list, or JCasC plus a plugin list file). Keep a staging controller restored from the production backup and apply updates there first. Take a `JENKINS_HOME` snapshot before each update.

#### Problem 3: the controller disk fills

**Scenario.** The Jenkins web interface returns errors, builds fail with "No space left on device".

**Symptoms.** `df -h` on the controller shows the partition holding `JENKINS_HOME` at 100 percent.

**Diagnosis.** The directory that holds most of the space is identified from the top downwards.

blocks.code:
$ df -h /var/lib/jenkins
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1        50G   50G     0 100% /
$ du -sh /var/lib/jenkins/* | sort -h | tail -3
2.1G    /var/lib/jenkins/plugins
9.4G    /var/lib/jenkins/workspace
36G     /var/lib/jenkins/jobs
$ du -sh /var/lib/jenkins/jobs/*/builds | sort -h | tail -2
4.8G    /var/lib/jenkins/jobs/orders-service/builds
27G     /var/lib/jenkins/jobs/legacy-release/builds
blocks.title: Find the largest directories (typical output, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** No build discarder was configured, so every build record and every archived artifact is kept forever; in addition, builds were allowed to run on the built-in node, which fills `workspace`.

**Fix.** Delete or archive the largest build histories, then configure the log rotation described below; move builds off the controller.

**Prevention.** `options { buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '20')) }` in every Jenkinsfile (the option appears on the jenkins.io pipeline syntax page), publish large artifacts to an artifact repository or registry rather than archiving them in Jenkins, zero executors on the built-in node, and a disk-usage alert on the controller volume.

#### Problem 4: builds queue for hours at peak time

**Scenario.** At the start of the working day the queue grows to dozens of builds and each waits for hours, although average utilization over the day is low.

**Symptoms.** All executors busy between roughly the same hours; the queue empties by the afternoon. **Diagnosis.** The queue page lists the waiting builds with the requested labels. Counting executors per label against the number of concurrent builds for that label shows the shortfall. A few long stages that hold an executor while waiting (a stage with `input`, a `sleep`, a deployment waiting on a rollout) are a common contributor.

**Root cause.** Capacity matches the daily average, not the peak, and executors are held by stages that do not use CPU.

**Fix.** Add agents, or move to Kubernetes or Docker clouds that create agents on demand. Move waiting for approvals out of agent allocation (a stage-level `input` runs before the stage's agent is allocated, as described in the next chapter).

**Prevention.** Measure queue time as a metric; set `disableConcurrentBuilds(abortPrevious: true)` for branch pipelines so that superseded builds of the same branch do not consume executors; use `timeout` options so that stuck builds release their executors.

### Questions to expect

1. **What is the difference between a controller, a node, an agent and an executor?** The controller is the Jenkins service that stores configuration, schedules and serves the UI. A node is a machine that can run work; an agent is the process on it that runs tasks for the controller; an executor is a slot (thread) on a node, so the executor count is the number of concurrent tasks.
2. **Why should builds not run on the built-in node?** Build steps would run inside the controller's process context and could read `JENKINS_HOME`, including credentials and keys; heavy builds also degrade the controller. The recommended setting is zero executors on the built-in node.
3. **Inbound agent or SSH agent?** The direction of connection differs. Inbound agents connect out to the controller (WebSocket or an enabled TCP port), which suits agents behind a firewall. SSH agents are started by the controller over SSH, which suits stable hosts reachable from the controller.
4. **What is an ephemeral agent and why use it?** An agent created for one build (a container or a Kubernetes pod) and discarded afterwards. Every build starts from the same image, which removes drift and leftover state, and capacity scales with demand.
5. **What lives in** `JENKINS_HOME` **and what must be backed up?** Configuration, job definitions, build records, credentials and their keys, plugins. Workspaces and caches can be recreated. The `master.key` is stored separately and securely.
6. **What is the difference between LTS and weekly releases?** Weekly releases carry new changes continuously; LTS is a baseline selected every 12 weeks and receives only backported fixes in three point releases. Production controllers normally follow LTS.
7. **What is a Multibranch Pipeline?** A project that scans a repository and creates a Pipeline job for each branch (and pull request, with a branch source plugin) that has a Jenkinsfile, so that the pipeline definition travels with the code.
8. **How is Jenkins configuration made reproducible?** With the Configuration as Code plugin (YAML applied at startup), a container image built with a fixed plugin list, Jenkinsfiles in source control and shared libraries; secrets are injected from the environment or a secret store.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Jenkins is a self-operated automation server: one controller holds configuration, queue, credentials and history, and agents run the work.

- Builds are matched to agents by label; executors are concurrent slots, and a build that cannot find a free matching executor waits in the queue.
- Zero executors on the built-in node, ephemeral agents and a short list of reviewed plugins limit the damage of a compromised or misbehaving build.
- Everything stateful sits in `JENKINS_HOME`; back it up, store `master.key` separately and discard old builds.
- Production controllers follow LTS releases and must run a supported Java (21 or 25 per the October 2026 documentation).
- Plugin updates are the most frequent cause of controller-wide breakage; test them on a staging controller first.

sections.title: The Jenkinsfile: Declarative Pipeline in Practice

blocks.text:
A job configured through forms in the web interface cannot be reviewed in a pull request, cannot be reproduced on a second controller and cannot be versioned together with the code it builds. Pipeline as code solves this: the build definition is a text file named `Jenkinsfile` stored in the repository root. A change to the build then travels through the same review, branching and history as a change to the application. The jenkins.io documentation on getting started with Pipeline states that defining the Pipeline in a `Jenkinsfile` loaded from source control is generally considered best practice.

This chapter defines the syntax of the Declarative Pipeline, explains where the code of a Jenkinsfile runs, develops a complete Jenkinsfile for `orders-service` (checkout, build, JUnit reports, SonarQube analysis, container image, deployment to staging, manual approval, deployment to production) and then covers the integration topics: webhooks, multibranch projects, credentials, shared libraries, configuration as code and upgrades. All Jenkinsfile listings are `illustrative configuration (not run)`: Jenkins was not available on the build machine. Their structure (balanced braces, directive nesting) was reviewed manually, and the syntax of each directive was compared with the jenkins.io pipeline syntax reference (consulted October 2026).

### Concept and mechanism

#### Declarative and scripted pipeline

Jenkins accepts two syntaxes in a Jenkinsfile. Both are domain-specific languages built on Groovy. The jenkins.io getting-started page presents the Declarative syntax first and places the Scripted form under an "Advanced" toggle, without stating a recommendation between the two; the preference for Declarative given below is a practical judgement, not a documented rule.

rows: Enforced and validated before the build starts; a syntax error fails fast
Free-form; errors appear when the faulty line executes
Readability for a new team member
High; the shape is the same in every repository
Complex dynamic logic, usually inside shared libraries

blocks.text: The directives used in this chapter, with the syntax as shown on the jenkins.io pipeline syntax page, are summarized below.

rows: `agent none` at top level means each stage must declare its own agent.
For username and password credentials, `KEY_USR` and `KEY_PSW` are also defined.
Pipeline-level only; the first run after adding a parameter has no UI form.
`H` spreads load by hashing the job name.
Declares tool installations configured under **Manage Jenkins \>** **Tools**
A wrapper such as `./mvnw` avoids the dependency.
Pauses the pipeline for a human decision.
Nested `stage` blocks run concurrently; `failFast true` aborts the siblings on first failure
`cleanup` runs last, after the other conditions.
blocks.caption: Declarative directives used in the orders-service pipeline.

blocks.text:
The page on running pipelines adds two operational features worth knowing: a completed Declarative run can be restarted from any top-level stage (inputs stay the same and a new build number is created), and `preserveStashes()` in `options` keeps stash contents for one to fifty completed runs (default one) so that such restarts can still unstash.

#### Where the code runs

A Jenkinsfile contains two kinds of code that run in different places, and confusing them is the root of several classic errors.

blocks.text:
The Pipeline Groovy is executed by the CPS (continuation-passing style) interpreter on the controller. Because of this transformation the controller can save the state of a running pipeline to a file called `program.dat` in the build directory and resume it after a restart (jenkins.io, CPS method mismatches page). A consequence is that every variable alive at the time a step is called has to be serializable, which leads to the first problem in the problems section. Methods annotated `@NonCPS` run with native Groovy semantics instead; they are faster and suit pure computation, but they must not call Pipeline steps such as `sh` or `node`. The same page lists further cautions: CPS closures passed to library methods that are not CPS-aware can give wrong results, and steps cannot be called from constructors.

#### Groovy needed to read a Jenkinsfile

Five Groovy constructs cover nearly every Jenkinsfile.

- **Strings.** `'single'` quotes are literal; `"double"` quotes interpolate `${expr}`; `'''triple single'''` spans lines and is literal. The difference matters for secrets (below).
- **Collections.** Lists `['a', 'b']` and maps `[key: 'value']`. A named-argument call such as `timeout(time: 10,` `unit: 'MINUTES')` passes a map.
- **Closures.** A block in braces passed to a step, such as the body of `timeout { ... }` or `withCredentials(...) {` `... }`.
- `def` **and typed variables.** `def x = 1` or `String x = 'a'`.
- **Elvis and safe navigation.** `cfg.profile ?: 'ci'` and `obj?.field`.

In a Declarative Pipeline, arbitrary Groovy statements are only allowed inside a `script { }` block, which should stay short.

#### When, input and agent: order of evaluation

Per the jenkins.io pipeline syntax page, the steps of the `options` directive are processed first, then an `input` directive pauses the stage before the stage's agent is allocated, then the agent is entered, and by default the `when` condition is evaluated after the agent is entered and after the options, but not before the `input`. Three flags change this: `beforeOptions true`, `beforeInput true` and `beforeAgent true` make the `when` condition be evaluated before the respective element, with `beforeOptions` taking precedence over `beforeInput`, which takes precedence over `beforeAgent`.

blocks.text:
Two practical rules follow. A deployment stage guarded by `when { branch 'main' }` and running on a scarce agent needs `beforeAgent true`, otherwise an executor is allocated on every branch only to skip the stage. An approval stage needs `beforeInput true`, otherwise every feature branch waits for a human. The second rule is easy to miss because the pipeline syntax reference states the default in one sentence only.

#### Credentials and string interpolation

Credentials are stored on the controller and are referenced by ID (see the previous chapter). Two ways bind them to a build, both described on the jenkins.io "Using a Jenkinsfile" page.

- The `credentials()` helper inside `environment` supports secret text, username with password and secret file. For a username-password credential named `SERVICE_CREDS`, the variables `SERVICE_CREDS_USR` and `SERVICE_CREDS_PSW` are defined. The placement of the `environment` block decides the scope: whole pipeline or one stage.
- The `withCredentials([...]) { ... }` step binds other types (SSH key, certificate, file) and is available only inside its block. The Snippet Generator in the classic UI produces the correct syntax.

Jenkins replaces the value of a bound credential with `****` in the console output. The documentation states that this only reduces accidental exposure, and it gives a firm rule: "Groovy string interpolation should never be used with credentials". A double-quoted `sh "curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer ${API_TOKEN}' ..."` makes Groovy substitute the secret into the command string on the controller, so it can appear in the process arguments on the agent and shell metacharacters inside it are executed. The safe form is single-quoted, so that the shell reads the variable from its environment: `sh 'curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ${API_TOKEN}" https://example.com'`. The same applies to user-supplied parameters, which can inject commands. The Jenkinsfile below follows this rule.

### Worked example: the complete Jenkinsfile for orders-service

The pipeline has the following shape: a CI stage on a `maven-jdk21` agent (build and test, then SonarQube analysis and dependency check in parallel, then the quality gate, then the container image for the `main` branch), followed by deployment to staging, a human approval and deployment to production.

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `agent none` at the top and an `agent` per stage. The approval stage has no agent, so the executor is released while a human decides. The jenkins.io getting-started page states that a top-level `agent` allocates an executor and workspace for the entire pipeline, which would hold an executor for up to 24 hours here.
- Nested `stages` under `stage('CI')` share one agent and one workspace, so the compiled classes and the `target` directory are available to every nested stage without stash and unstash.
- `junit` in a `post { always }` block publishes test results even when a test fails; with the unit and integration test reports under `target/*-reports`, the glob matches the JUnit XML files only (`TEST-*.xml`) and not the Failsafe summary file.
- `waitForQualityGate abortPipeline: true` pauses until the SonarQube result arrives by webhook. Per the SonarQube documentation (consulted October 2026), the webhook from SonarQube to `<jenkins>/sonarqube-webhook/` is mandatory, the step does not poll or occupy a node, it survives a Jenkins restart, and it should be wrapped in `timeout`. In this file the step sits in a stage whose agent is already allocated, so the executor is held for the wait (at most 10 minutes). A pipeline that must release the executor places the gate in a separate stage with `agent none`.
- `env.IMAGE_TAG` is assigned inside a `script` block and read by later stages: assignments to `env` persist for the rest of the build, across agents. The tag is the short commit hash, so every image is traceable to a commit and tags are never reused.
- Credentials: `withCredentials` with single-quoted shell text. `docker login --password-stdin` keeps the token out of the process list. The kubeconfig is bound as a file and exposed through the `KUBECONFIG` variable, which `kubectl` reads.
- `disableConcurrentBuilds(abortPrevious: true)` aborts a running build of the same branch when a newer commit starts one, which saves executors in a multibranch setup.
- `beforeAgent true` on the deployment stages and `beforeInput true` on the approval stage follow the evaluation rules above.

The pipeline deploys with `kubectl set image` to a Deployment named `orders-service` whose container is named `app`; the Kubernetes objects are defined in the part of this guide on running in production, and `kubectl rollout status` makes the stage fail if the new pods do not become ready within 180 seconds.

The same pipeline written as a GitHub Actions workflow is shown in the comparison chapter that follows this one.

### Triggers, integration and operation

#### Webhooks and polling

A build can start by schedule, by polling the repository, or by a push notification. Polling (`pollSCM('H/5 * * * *')`) makes the controller query the repository at intervals; it adds load and delays builds by up to one interval. A webhook makes the repository host send an HTTP request when something changes. With the GitHub plugin, the endpoint is `$JENKINS_URL/github-webhook/`; one URL serves all repositories, and the job must have the trigger "GitHub hook trigger for GITScm polling" enabled. Because the endpoint is publicly reachable in the usual case, Jenkins confirms with GitHub that a push actually occurred before acting (plugin documentation, consulted October 2026). Behind a firewall, an override hook URL through a reverse proxy can be configured. Multibranch and organization folder projects based on the GitHub Branch Source plugin receive events from the same mechanism and re-scan on demand; without webhooks, the multibranch documentation recommends periodic indexing (the example uses 30 minutes).

blocks.text: The first step of this sequence can be reproduced without Jenkins. A bare repository acts as the remote, and a `post-receive` hook plays the role of the webhook receiver. The hook below only prints; a real receiver would enqueue a build. This run was executed on the build machine with git 2.43.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# Simulated CI trigger: runs after every push, like a webhook receiver.
while read old new ref; do
  branch=${ref#refs/heads/}
  echo "[ci] push received: branch=$branch commit=${new:0:7}"
  echo "[ci] build queued for $branch"
done
blocks.title: remote.git/hooks/post-receive (simulated webhook receiver)

blocks.code:
$ git push origin main
remote: [ci] push received: branch=main commit=8215dc3
remote: [ci] build queued for main
To /tmp/dvw_v4/hook/remote.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
blocks.title: Push to the bare repository (real output)

blocks.text:
The output shows the essential property of the mechanism: the remote side learns the branch name and commit hash at push time, and it can start work immediately. A hosted webhook replaces the hook script with an HTTPS POST to Jenkins.

For GitHub integration, the Jenkins side needs credentials to read repositories and to report statuses. The GitHub Branch Source plugin documentation links to a guide for authentication as a GitHub App, which gives fine-grained permissions and a higher rate limit than a personal access token (from memory, verify before use). The page on the plugin did not describe the procedure in the text that could be read, so that guide is the source to follow.

#### Shared libraries

When ten services carry near-identical Jenkinsfiles, a fix has to be repeated ten times. A shared library moves common code into a separate Git repository that Jenkinsfiles load by name and version.

blocks.text: Per the jenkins.io shared libraries page, `vars/` holds scripts exposed as global variables (the file name becomes the step name), `src/` holds Groovy classes on the classpath and `resources/` holds non-Groovy files read through `libraryResource`. The annotation forms are `@Library('name') _`, `@Library('name@1.0') _` and a list form; the underscore is used when only global variables are needed. A library is configured globally under **Manage Jenkins \>** **System** (global libraries can be marked trusted, which requires the Overall/RunScripts permission) or per folder (folder libraries are always untrusted and run in the Groovy sandbox). Pinning a tag, as in the example, makes a change to the library an explicit, reviewable upgrade of each consumer.

Jenkinsfile using the library (illustrative configuration, not run)

blocks.text:
The page states that in a Declarative Pipeline, method calls on a library variable such as `log.info 'Starting'` must be wrapped in a `script` block; a global variable defined with a `call` method, as above, is invoked like an ordinary step. Library code runs through the same CPS interpreter, so the same serialization rules apply.

#### Visualization, configuration as code and upgrades

The Blue Ocean plugin page marks the plugin as deprecated: it "will not receive further functionality updates" and only selective updates for significant security or functional defects, and the Pipeline Stage View and Pipeline Graph View plugins are named as partial replacements (consulted October 2026). New installations should therefore not be designed around it.

Configuration as code was introduced in the previous chapter. The practical pattern is three artifacts in one repository: the JCasC YAML, a plugin list, and a container image build that installs exactly those plugins. A new controller is then reproducible from Git, and an upgrade is a pull request that builds a new image, which is started against the existing `JENKINS_HOME` volume. Upgrade procedure (the jenkins.io upgrade page could not be fetched while preparing this guide, so the order below is general practice, from memory, verify before use): back up `JENKINS_HOME` (and keep `master.key` separately), read the changelog and upgrade guide for every version crossed, confirm that the Java version on the host is supported by the target release, upgrade a staging copy restored from the backup first, then upgrade the core, then the plugins that the core upgrade reports as outdated, and run a representative set of pipelines before declaring the upgrade complete. Security advisories published by the project name the fixed versions; the advisory index lists them with their dates.

### Hands-on

Objective: build a small pipeline that exercises `parallel`, `post`, `when` and `input`, and observe the executor behaviour.

1. In a repository with a Maven project (any small project works), create a `Jenkinsfile` with `agent none`, one stage `Build` (agent label of an available agent, step `sh 'mvn -B -q verify'`) and a `post { failure { echo 'failed' }` `}` block. Create a Pipeline job from SCM and run it.
2. Add a `Checks` stage with two parallel nested stages, each printing a message and sleeping 20 seconds (`sleep 20`). Confirm in the stage view that both run concurrently and that the wall-clock time is about 20 seconds, not 40.
3. Add a stage `Approve` with `input { message 'Continue?' }` and no agent, followed by a stage `Deploy` that only echoes text. Run the build, leave it paused, and open **Manage Jenkins \> Nodes**: the executor used by `Build` is free while the build waits.
4. Add `when { branch 'main' }` to `Approve` without `beforeInput true`. Run the pipeline on a feature branch of a Multibranch project. The build pauses for approval although the stage should be skipped. Add `beforeInput true` and run again; the stage is now skipped.
5. Make `Build` fail deliberately (for example `sh 'exit 1'`). Confirm that the `post { failure }` block runs and that later stages are skipped.

Expected result: concurrent wall-clock time of the parallel stages, an idle executor during the pause, and the skipped approval stage after the flag was added. This behaviour follows the documented evaluation order, but it was not observed on the build machine.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 5: a credential appears in the console output

**Scenario.** A team member finds a registry token in a build log that is readable by all authenticated users.

**Symptoms.** The log shows the token text (or a Base64 form of it) in a `curl` command line, a `docker login` line or the output of `env`.

**Diagnosis.** Search the console output for the secret value. Review the Jenkinsfile for double-quoted `sh "..."` strings containing `${...}` of a credential variable, for `echo` of environment variables, for `set -x` in shell steps and for `printenv`. Masking only replaces the exact bound value; a transformed value (Base64, URL-encoded, a substring) is not masked.

**Root cause.** The secret was interpolated by Groovy into the command string, or a script transformed the value before printing it, so the masking rule no longer matched. The documentation states that masking only reduces accidental exposure.

**Fix.** Revoke and replace the credential at the issuing service immediately; deleting the log line does not undo the exposure. Delete or restrict the affected build logs. Correct the step to single quotes with environment variable expansion and `--password-stdin`.

**Prevention.** Single-quoted shell text for every step that uses credentials; no `set -x` in those steps; separate credentials per environment with the minimum scope; folder-level credentials so that only the owning team's jobs can use them; never allow untrusted pull request pipelines (forks) to use trusted credentials, as the jenkins.io documentation warns.

#### Problem 6: a pipeline waits for input and never finishes

**Scenario.** A build has been running for three days; the executor and a workspace are held.

**Symptoms.** The stage view shows a paused stage with a "Proceed or Abort" prompt; the queue grows because the executor is occupied.

**Diagnosis.** The paused build page shows the input prompt, the submitter restriction and the elapsed time. If the `input` stage is inside a stage with an agent that was allocated earlier, **Nodes** shows the executor in use by that build. **Root cause.** The pipeline has no timeout on the approval, the people allowed by `submitter` are on leave or the name in `submitter` does not match any account, and the top-level `agent` keeps an executor allocated during the wait.

**Fix.** Abort the build from the UI. Add `options { timeout(time: 24, unit: 'HOURS') }` to the approval stage and correct the submitter list (user names or group names separated by commas).

**Prevention.** `agent none` at the top and no agent on the approval stage, a timeout on every `input`, and a notification (chat or e-mail) when the pipeline reaches the approval so that approvers notice.

#### Problem 7: the webhook does not start builds

**Scenario.** Pushes to GitHub no longer start builds; builds only start when someone clicks "Build now".

**Symptoms.** The webhook page in the GitHub repository settings shows recent deliveries with a red mark (timeout, 403, 404 or 5xx), or no deliveries at all.

**Diagnosis.** Open the webhook's recent deliveries and read the response code and body. A timeout or connection error points to the network path (firewall, reverse proxy, a changed DNS name). A 403 points to a CSRF or authentication problem on the endpoint. A 404 points to a wrong path (the GitHub plugin endpoint ends with `/github-webhook/`, including the trailing slash). Use the "Test hook" button that the plugin documentation mentions, and enable logging for `com.cloudbees.jenkins.GitHubPushTrigger` and `org.jenkinsci.plugins.github.webhook.WebhookManager` to see what the controller received. For a Multibranch project, check that the repository's scan log shows the event.

**Root cause.** Typical causes are a Jenkins URL changed or protected by a new reverse proxy without forwarding the path; the job missing the "GitHub hook trigger for GITScm polling" setting; the controller unreachable from the internet because the installation is on a private network; and the secret or credentials used by the plugin to manage hooks having expired.

**Fix.** Correct the URL or route, re-enable the trigger, and redeliver a failed delivery from the GitHub page. For a controller that cannot be reached from the internet, use an override hook URL through a relay, or fall back to polling or periodic multibranch indexing until networking is changed.

**Prevention.** A synthetic check that alerts when no build has started for a repository with recent commits; periodic indexing as a safety net of low frequency.

#### Problem 8: a Groovy serialization error ends the build

**Scenario.** A build that works for months fails after a small change that extracts the version from `pom.xml` with a regular expression.

**Symptoms.** (typical output, not run on the build machine; from memory, verify before use)

**Console output of a CPS serialization failure (typical, not run)**

blocks.code: java.io.NotSerializableException: java.util.regex.Matcher

blocks.text:
**Diagnosis.** The error names a class that cannot be serialized. Find the variable of that type that was alive when a step ran (here the `Matcher` in a local variable).

**Root cause.** The CPS interpreter must be able to save all live variables when a step is executed. A `Matcher`, an iterator or a database connection is not serializable, so the save fails at the next step call. This is the consequence of the design described in the CPS documentation (state is saved to `program.dat`).

blocks.title: Broken: a live Matcher variable at the time of the next step (illustrative)

blocks.text: **Fix.** Confine the non-serializable object to a `@NonCPS` method that returns a plain value, and call that method.

blocks.title: Fixed: the Matcher never lives in pipeline code (illustrative)

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Keep pipeline Groovy short; move parsing and computation into `@NonCPS` helpers or into the build tool (for the project version, `mvn help:evaluate -Dexpression=project.version -q -DforceStdout` returns it without regular expressions); prefer `readMavenPom` or `readJSON` style steps where a plugin supplies them (from memory, verify before use); never call Pipeline steps inside `@NonCPS` methods, which the documentation lists as anomalous behaviour.

### Questions to expect

1. **Declarative or scripted pipeline, and why?** Declarative has a fixed, validated structure and fails fast on syntax errors, which makes pipelines uniform across repositories. Scripted allows arbitrary Groovy and is used for dynamic logic, usually inside a shared library. Declarative accepts Groovy in `script` blocks as an escape hatch.
2. **Where does the Groovy in a Jenkinsfile execute?** On the controller, through the CPS interpreter. Steps such as `sh` run on the agent. For that reason variables must be serializable and heavy computation does not belong in pipeline Groovy.
3. **What does** `agent none` **at the top level do?** No executor is allocated for the pipeline as a whole; each stage declares its own agent. It allows stages such as `input` to wait without holding an executor.
4. **Why is** `beforeAgent true` **used with** `when`**?** By default `when` is evaluated after the agent is allocated. With the flag, a false condition skips the stage without allocating an executor. `beforeInput true` does the same for a stage with an `input` directive.
5. **How are secrets used safely in a Jenkinsfile?** Bound with `credentials()` or `withCredentials` and read in single-quoted shell text, so the shell expands the variable and Groovy never sees the value. Masking in the log is a safety net only.
6. **Webhook or polling?** A webhook notifies Jenkins when something changes and avoids repeated queries and delay; polling is a fallback when Jenkins cannot be reached from the repository host. Multibranch projects combine webhooks with periodic indexing.
7. **What is a shared library and why pin its version?** A Git repository of Groovy steps, classes and resources loaded with `@Library`. Pinning a tag makes a library change a deliberate upgrade of each pipeline instead of an immediate change to all of them.
8. **How can an unfinished approval hold up a Jenkins installation?** A top-level agent keeps an executor allocated while the pipeline waits. Remedies are `agent none` with per-stage agents, a `timeout` on the approval and notifications to the approvers.
9. **What does a Multibranch Pipeline add over a single Pipeline job?** Automatic creation of a job per branch and pull request that contains a Jenkinsfile, with branch and change identifiers in `BRANCH_NAME` and `CHANGE_ID`, so that conditional logic such as deploying only from `main` can be written in the file.
10. **What is the purpose of** `post` **and which conditions exist?** Steps that run after the stages: `always`, `success`, `failure`, `unstable`, `changed` and `cleanup` (last). Typical uses are publishing test reports, notifications and workspace cleanup.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A Jenkinsfile in the repository makes the build reviewable and versioned; Declarative syntax gives a fixed structure, `script` blocks and shared libraries cover the rest.

- Groovy statements run on the controller (CPS); `sh` and similar steps run on the agent. Live variables must be serializable; use `@NonCPS` for parsing.
- Use `agent none` plus stage agents so that `input` waits without an executor; add `beforeInput true` and `beforeAgent` `true` where a `when` guard must run first.
- Credentials belong in `credentials()` or `withCredentials`, read through single-quoted shell text; Groovy string interpolation of secrets is forbidden by the documentation.
- `waitForQualityGate` needs the SonarQube webhook to Jenkins and a `timeout`; webhooks are preferred to polling.
- Shared libraries remove duplication across services; pin their version. Blue Ocean is deprecated.

sections.title: Why Jenkins When GitHub Has Actions

blocks.text:
A frequent question from people who learn continuous integration today is the following: GitHub already provides CI/CD in the form of GitHub Actions, so why does Jenkins still appear in job descriptions, in company pipelines and in this guide? The question is reasonable, and the answer is neither "Jenkins is obsolete" nor "Actions is a toy". Both tools run builds, tests and deployments from a definition stored in the repository. They differ in who operates the coordinating server, which source control systems and networks they can reach, how they are paid for, how far they can be customized and what already exists in a given organization.

The short answer, which the rest of the chapter substantiates, is the following. For a project hosted on GitHub whose team does not want to operate a server (most startups, most open-source projects, most student projects), GitHub Actions is usually sufficient and usually the better first choice. Jenkins is chosen when one or more of these conditions hold: the organization already runs a large Jenkins installation; the code or the builds must stay inside a private network; the repositories are spread over several source control systems; the pipelines need customization that a hosted service does not offer; or the cost and limits of a metered service are unacceptable at the organization's scale. The two tools are also not mutually exclusive: Jenkins can be started by a GitHub webhook, and a GitHub Actions workflow can call Jenkins.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Tool names, plans, prices and limits in this area change frequently. The facts in this chapter were checked against docs.github.com, jenkins.io and the vendor pages named in the text in October 2026, and each is stated with its source. Examples of change within a single year: GitHub announced a platform charge for self-hosted runners and then postponed it; the Jenkins X project is now presented under the name JayeX; Atlassian announced the end of life of Bamboo Data Center. Before a decision, the current documentation must be read again. Statements marked `from` `memory, verify before use` were not checked.

### Concept and mechanism

#### What each tool is

**GitHub Actions** is a CI/CD service built into GitHub. A workflow is a YAML file in `.github/workflows/` of a repository; it is triggered by repository events (push, pull request, release, schedule, manual dispatch, and others) and consists of jobs that run on runners. A runner is either a virtual machine provided by GitHub (GitHub-hosted) or a machine operated by the user (self-hosted). The server side (workflow engine, queue, logs, user interface, secret storage) is operated by GitHub.

**Jenkins** is an open-source automation server (jenkins.io documentation) that is installed and operated by the team that uses it. A controller holds configuration, queue and history; agents run the work; plugins add integrations. A pipeline is defined in a `Jenkinsfile` (Groovy-based) or in job configuration in the UI. The previous two chapters describe the architecture and the syntax.

The decisive structural difference is the second sentence of each paragraph: the coordinating server is a service in one case and a system to be run in the other. Most other differences follow from it.

blocks.text:
#### Who is responsible for what

Operating a CI system consists of several layers of work, and each tool places the boundary between provider and team in a different position.

blocks.text:
Three facts from docs.github.com support the middle column. GitHub-hosted runners are new virtual machines for each job (except single-CPU runners, which run in a container on a shared VM), maintained and updated by GitHub, with the preinstalled software refreshed weekly. For self-hosted runners, GitHub states that automatic updates cover only the runner application, and that the user is responsible for the operating system and other software. The runner software itself is free; the user pays for the machines.

#### Comparison

The three tables below compare the tools on the dimensions that normally decide the question. A cell states what the documentation supports; cells marked `from memory` were not verified in October 2026.

blocks.text:
#### Cost model with an explicit calculation

A fair cost comparison has to include people. The structure is simple: the cost of GitHub Actions is the number of billed minutes above the included amount multiplied by the rate; the cost of Jenkins is largely fixed (machines plus the administrator's time) and grows in steps as agents are added. The following script computes both. The rate (0.006 USD per minute for a Linux 2-core runner) and the included minutes (3000 per month on the Team plan) come from the GitHub billing page consulted in October 2026; every other input is **assumed** and must be replaced by the organization's own numbers. The script was run on the build machine; the arithmetic is real, the inputs are not measurements.

blocks.code:
# Break-even sketch. Every input below is ASSUMED, except the per-minute rate and the included
# minutes, which are taken from the GitHub billing page (consulted October 2026).
RATE_LINUX_2CORE = 0.006      # USD per minute, GitHub-hosted Linux 2-core
INCLUDED_TEAM = 3000          # minutes per month, GitHub Team plan

def actions_cost(minutes):
    return max(0, minutes - INCLUDED_TEAM) * RATE_LINUX_2CORE

AGENT_VM = 70.0               # assumed USD per month for one build VM
AGENTS = 2                    # assumed
ADMIN_HOURS = 6               # assumed hours per month for patching, plugins, backups
ADMIN_RATE = 50.0             # assumed USD per hour of engineer time

def jenkins_cost():
    return AGENTS * AGENT_VM + ADMIN_HOURS * ADMIN_RATE

fixed = jenkins_cost()
print("Jenkins fixed monthly cost (assumed inputs): %.2f USD" % fixed)
for builds in (500, 3000, 10000, 40000):
    minutes = builds * 8      # assumed 8 minutes per build
    print("builds=%6d minutes=%7d actions=%8.2f jenkins=%7.2f"
          % (builds, minutes, actions_cost(minutes), fixed))
be = fixed / RATE_LINUX_2CORE + INCLUDED_TEAM
print("break-even minutes per month: %.0f (about %.0f builds of 8 minutes)"
      % (be, be / 8))

blocks.text:
Three conclusions follow from the structure rather than from the numbers. First, at low volume the metered service is cheaper by a wide margin, because the fixed cost of operating Jenkins does not shrink. Second, at high volume a fixed-cost system wins, but only until it needs more agents and more administrator time, so the Jenkins line is a staircase and not a flat line (the script treats it as flat, which favours Jenkins at the highest volume). Third, an organization can also run Actions on its own machines: the billing page states that usage on self-hosted runners is free, so Actions with self-hosted runners removes the per-minute cost but keeps the machine cost. GitHub announced in December 2025 a charge of 0.002 USD per minute for self-hosted runner usage starting March 2026, and its page of 15 December 2025 states that this billing change is postponed with no new date given; GitHub Enterprise Server was not affected. Whether the charge returns is not known, which is a reason to check the billing page before relying on a free self-hosted model.

#### Scale and concurrency

On GitHub-hosted runners, concurrency is bounded by the plan (20 concurrent jobs on Free up to 500 on Enterprise, per the usage limits page), and a job may run for at most 6 hours. For most application teams these bounds are not binding. They matter for organizations with hundreds of engineers on one organization account, for long-running test suites (hardware simulation, large integration environments) and for burst patterns where a release triggers thousands of jobs. Larger runners and self-hosted runners lift some of these limits, and concurrency limits can be raised through GitHub Support (as the limits page states for job concurrency). Jenkins has no such product limit, but capacity has to be built: a queue that grows at peak time (the fourth problem in the architecture chapter) is the Jenkins equivalent of hitting a plan limit.

#### Security, compliance and private networks

The strongest and most frequent reason for Jenkins in large organizations is not a missing feature but a constraint on where code and builds may live. Several distinct cases must be separated.

- **No SaaS permitted.** Banks, defence contractors and public-sector bodies often forbid sending source code to an external service. Jenkins on premises satisfies this directly. GitHub Enterprise Server also satisfies it: Actions on GHES uses self-hosted runners only, the official actions are bundled with the server, and the `actions-sync` tool supports air-gapped installations (docs.github.com, consulted October 2026). The argument "regulated, therefore Jenkins" is therefore incomplete; "regulated and not using GHES" is the accurate form.
- **Builds must reach internal systems.** A build that deploys to servers in a private data center, reads from an internal artifact repository or talks to a mainframe needs network access that a GitHub-hosted runner does not have. A self-hosted runner inside the network solves it for Actions. The runner needs outbound HTTPS on port 443 only; docs.github.com states no inbound connection requirement.
- **Data residency and audit.** Where logs and artifacts are stored, and who can read them, can be a legal requirement. Both tools can meet it when self-hosted; the evidence needed by auditors (who approved which deployment, which commit was deployed) comes from the approval mechanism and the retention settings in either tool.
- **Supply-chain exposure.** Marketplace actions are third-party code executed with the workflow's permissions; GitHub's secure-use guidance advises pinning actions to a full-length commit SHA, limiting `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions and avoiding script injection. Jenkins plugins run with the full privileges of the controller, and the advisory index shows frequent advisories. Neither model is free of this risk; the difference is that the Jenkins administrator carries the patching duty directly.
- **Self-hosted runner risk.** GitHub states that self-hosted runners can be persistently compromised by untrusted code in a workflow and should almost never be used for public repositories. The same reasoning applies to Jenkins agents building pull requests from forks.

#### Several source control systems, and non-Git work

Jenkins decouples the CI server from the source control host. An organization with code in GitHub, an internal GitLab, Bitbucket and a legacy Subversion or Perforce server can run all pipelines in one Jenkins installation with one set of credentials, approvals and reports. GitHub Actions is triggered by GitHub events; for code hosted elsewhere, it would need mirroring or an external trigger. GitLab CI/CD and Azure Pipelines are similar to Actions in this respect (each is tied to its own platform, though Azure Pipelines supports GitHub and Azure Repos per Microsoft documentation). Work that is not a software build at all (nightly data jobs, hardware-in-the-loop test benches attached to specific machines, mainframe batch submissions) is also a traditional Jenkins use, because an agent can be placed on any machine that can run Java and then selected by label. Actions self-hosted runners can reach the same machines, so this is an advantage only where the rest of the Jenkins estate already exists.

#### Legacy investment and migration cost

An organization with 300 Jenkins jobs, 40 shared library steps, years of credentials, approval rules and reporting built on plugin features has made an investment that a migration must repay. Migration cost is not the YAML conversion; it is the re-creation of behaviour that was implemented through plugins, the re-validation of every pipeline, the retraining of teams and the period of running two systems. GitHub offers GitHub Actions Importer, which supports Jenkins among other systems, and its documentation states that converted workflows are not guaranteed to be correct, that each must be inspected before production use, and that the target conversion rate is 80 percent per workflow, depending on the pipeline. That figure is a design target of the tool and not a measured outcome for any particular estate.

#### The maintenance burden of Jenkins

The honest counterweight to all of the above is the cost of keeping Jenkins healthy. Core upgrades follow a 12-week baseline rhythm and Java support windows (Java 17 support ended with LTS 2.541.3 in March 2026 per the Java support policy page). Plugins need updates, and advisories name several plugins several times per year. Controllers need backups that are restore-tested, disk monitoring and an owner. The typical failure of Jenkins in practice is organizational: a controller with no owner, plugin versions frozen because nobody dares to update, and pipelines that only one departed engineer understood. The problems at the end of this chapter and of the architecture chapter describe the consequences.

#### When each is the sensible choice

#### Alternatives

Jenkins and Actions are two of many CI/CD tools. The one-line descriptions below were taken from the vendors' own pages in October 2026 unless marked.

rows: Pipelines defined in `.gitlab-ci.yml`, executed by runners; available on GitLab Self-Managed, GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated (docs.gitlab.com).
Natural choice when the code is already in GitLab.
The CI/CD service of Azure DevOps; works with GitHub and Azure Repos; agents can be self-hosted (Microsoft Learn).
Hosted CI/CD platform with pipelines in `config.yml`, and runner documentation for own infrastructure (circleci.com/docs).
A commercial service comparable in model to Actions.
Server product like Jenkins; details on licensing and SCM support not verified here.
Atlassian CI server. Atlassian lists Bamboo Data Center in its Data Center end-of-life announcement: new customers could not buy after 30 March 2026, end of life is 28 March 2029 (atlassian.com).
Existing installations migrate to other tools.
Cloud-native CI/CD building blocks that run as Kubernetes custom resources (Task, Pipeline); CNCF incubating project (tekton.dev).
Kubernetes-native; a framework more than a product.
Container-native workflow engine on Kubernetes; each step is a container, steps in sequence or as a DAG (Argo documentation).
Often used for data and batch workflows as well as CI.
Kubernetes-based CI/CD with GitOps and Tekton pipelines; the project page announces the new name JayeX.
Separate from Jenkins despite the name.

The question is often posed as a choice, but the tools combine. Three patterns occur in practice.

blocks.text:
1. **GitHub triggers Jenkins.** A webhook (the GitHub plugin endpoint `/github-webhook/`) or a branch source plugin starts the Jenkins pipeline on a push or pull request. This is the standard integration described in the previous chapter.
2. **Actions calls Jenkins.** A workflow step triggers a Jenkins job through its remote API, for example `curl -X POST` `-u "$JENKINS_USER:$JENKINS_TOKEN"` `"$JENKINS_URL/job/orders-deploy/buildWithParameters?VERSION=$GITHUB_SHA"` (job URL format and API-token authentication from memory, verify before use). This keeps the existing deployment pipelines while checks move to Actions. The Jenkins URL must be reachable from the runner; a self-hosted runner in the same network satisfies that.
3. **Jenkins calls Actions.** The REST endpoint `POST` `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/dispatches` with a body containing `ref` (and optional `inputs`) starts a workflow that declares the `workflow_dispatch` trigger. A fine-grained token needs the Actions repository permission set to write (docs.github.com REST reference, consulted October 2026).

A hybrid is not a stable end state by itself, because two systems double the credentials, the audit trail and the knowledge needed. It is a reasonable transition state, and sometimes a permanent boundary: public-cloud checks in Actions, deployment inside the private network in Jenkins.

### Worked example: the same pipeline in both tools

The orders-service pipeline of the previous chapter is shown here as a GitHub Actions workflow. The mapping of concepts comes first, because it is the part that transfers to any other pair of tools.

rows: One repository may hold several workflow files.
Labels choose self-hosted runners; hosted runners are chosen by image name.
Jobs run on separate runners; sharing files between jobs needs artifacts or caches, not a shared workspace.
Nested sequential stages on one agent
Parallelism is the default between jobs.
There is no separate post block.
Group key chosen by the author.
At workflow, job or step level.
Secrets are masked in logs; secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forks (from memory, verify before use).
Private repositories require a paid plan for this; the wait is limited (30 days per limits page).
Reusable workflows are called from a job with `uses:`.
Test report upload or a third-party action
Test trend history is not built in (from memory, verify before use).
Retention and storage are subject to plan limits.
No polling configuration; events are native to GitHub.

blocks.code:
name: orders-service CI/CD
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
permissions:
  contents: read
env:
  REGISTRY: ghcr.io
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '21'
          cache: maven
      - run: ./mvnw -B verify
      - name: SonarQube analysis
        run: ./mvnw -B sonar:sonar -Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true
        env:
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
          SONAR_HOST_URL: ${{ vars.SONAR_HOST_URL }}
      - name: Dependency-Check
        run: ./mvnw -B org.owasp:dependency-check-maven:check
        env:
          NVD_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.NVD_API_KEY }}
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()
        with:
          name: test-reports
          path: target/*-reports/
  image:
    needs: build
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ github.repository_owner }}/orders-service:${{ github.sha }}
deploy-staging:
  needs: image
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  environment: staging
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v7
    - run: ./deploy.sh staging ${{ github.sha }}
      env:
        KUBE_CONFIG: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG }}
deploy-production:
  needs: deploy-staging
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  environment: production
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v7
    - run: ./deploy.sh production ${{ github.sha }}
      env:
        KUBE_CONFIG: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG }}
blocks.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml (illustrative configuration, not run; syntax checked with PyYAML)

blocks.text: Action versions in the listing (`actions/checkout@v7`, `actions/setup-java@v6`, `actions/upload-artifact@v7`, `docker/login-action@v4`, `docker/build-push-action@v7`) were read from the releases pages of the respective repositories in October 2026 and are major tags. A production workflow pins actions to a full-length commit SHA, per the GitHub security guidance cited above. The `-Dsonar.qualitygate.wait=true` property makes the SonarScanner for Maven wait for the quality gate (from memory, verify before use). The workflow runs the Sonar analysis and the dependency check inside the single `build` job, whereas the Jenkinsfile ran them in parallel; splitting them into separate jobs restores the parallelism at the cost of a second checkout and build.

blocks.code:
$ python3 -I -c "import yaml; d=yaml.safe_load(open('ci.yml')); print(list(d['jobs']))"
['build', 'image', 'deploy-staging', 'deploy-production']
$ python3 -I -c "import yaml; d=yaml.safe_load(open('ci.yml')); print(list(d))"
['name', True, 'concurrency', 'permissions', 'env', 'jobs']
blocks.title: Syntax check of the workflow with PyYAML (real output)

blocks.text:
The second command shows a detail of YAML 1.1 parsers: the key `on` is parsed as the boolean `True`. GitHub's own parser treats it as the event key, so the file is correct; the effect is only visible when a Python script inspects the file, and a validation script must look up `d[True]`. PyYAML checks syntax only; it does not know the workflow schema, so keys misspelled in a way that is still valid YAML are not detected. An editor extension or a linter that knows the schema is the next level of checking.

blocks.text:
The sequence in the figure reduces to five questions that can be asked in any organization. In order of weight they are:

1. Do constraints on location (on-premises code, closed networks, data residency) exclude a hosted service? If yes, the candidates are Jenkins and GitHub Enterprise Server with self-hosted runners.
2. Is the code in more than one SCM system or outside GitHub? If yes, a CI server independent of the SCM, or the CI feature of the platform that hosts the code (GitLab CI/CD for GitLab), fits better than Actions.
3. Does a working Jenkins estate exist? If yes, the benefit of migrating must exceed the migration cost; the default is to keep it and to avoid building new pipelines in a style that is hard to move.
4. Is a special network, hardware or compliance boundary needed? If yes, self-hosted runners or Jenkins agents are needed; the choice then depends on skills and on the CI server already in use.
5. Otherwise, hosted Actions with GitHub-hosted runners is the lowest-effort option.

A written decision should also record the factors that are not in the sequence: the team's existing skills (a team that knows Groovy and Jenkins administration is faster with Jenkins at first), the support model (a managed service has a vendor to call; a self-operated server has colleagues), and the planned lifetime of the system.

#### Migration path

A migration from Jenkins to Actions is a project with phases, not a conversion run.
